utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning again, Your Honours. General Petkovic's Defence has prepared its presentation in PowerPoint. Given the fact that our Trial Chamber preferred to receive hard copies no matter what we presented to them, we also prepared hard copies for you as well of the material to be presented in court. We also provided the OPT with a copy so that they can see clearly what it was that we put on paper and so that they could prepare their response. Just a brief remark before I start. You will observe that some parts of the text in PowerPoint have been mark in the blue; those are our comments. The words in red are the documents that are protected. Slides with such documents should not be broadcast outside the courtroom. That is how we can protect the confidentiality of such documents. We can see on the slides what the topics discussed by General Petkovic's Defence will deal with today. These are rather simple topics as it appears, no matter how complex legally speaking. The first one is only one single common criminal purpose of ethnic cleansing. The second topic deals directly with Milivoje Petkovic and his decisions and participation in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Before I start analysing the judgement itself, we wanted to show you the seven questions we believe to be crucial when findings are made in this case. We wanted to show you this because these are our positions that we base our arguments and conclusions on. The first topic are the so-called alleged political or criminal goals. Both the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber in the Martic case established that a political intent to unite territories with similar ethnic composition in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia and their unification with Serbia is not a crime in and of itself. By this political goal alone, one cannot meet the standard of criminal proceedings. This was similarly expressed in the Seselj case and this is the position of General Petkovic's Defence as well. That is why we will not deal with political goal, topics, and discussions; we will deal with specific events. On the next slide, we can see the jurisprudence concerning the mens rea requisite for the existence of a JCE. That is to say, the intent to take part in the furtherance of a criminal plan. It has to be the only reasonable inference that can be concluded from the evidence. The next slide are rules concerning the circumstantial case based on indicia alone. I just wanted to remind you that my learned friend Mr. Khan in his presentation drew your attention several times to the way findings are made in a circumstantial case. All of these are the positions of the Appeals Chamber. We only wanted to remind you of these because we wanted to show that the conclusions of the of the Trial Chamber and its majority were not the only reasonable inference. The findings they made were not reasonable whatsoever, let alone being the only reasonable inference based on facts presented. The following slide indicates the position of the Tribunal in the Kupreskic case concerning the context of certain events during which crimes were committed. During our trial, we frequently encountered the prohibition of our Trial Chamber to pose certain questions as to the context. The explanation provided was that the tu quoque defence was impermissible. Based on the position expressed here, as was the position of all of the Defences in this case, we wanted to point out the importance of the context, not to justify the crimes, but to prove that certain events were not the result of criminal intent. They were simply a result of what was going on in the field. The next topic that is crucial, in particular for my client, is the topic of initial and continuing detention. The initial detention of military-aged men is something that as viewed by the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal is seen as permissible, under the condition that it needs to be established in a timely manner whether such military-aged men are civilian or not. If they are civilians, whether they represent a security threat; if they do not, such men need to be released from detention. This position is completely in accordance with a comment made in the Fourth Geneva Conventions, and I cite the footnote and the page, of commentary. It reads: "Men of military age could represent a security threat for the purpose of security detention where there is a danger of him being able to join the enemy armed forces." This is crucial to view the events which took place on the 30th of June, 1993. The next topic deals with ethnic balance and whether it should or should not be changed if there is a criminal plan in existence of ethnic cleansing. If it needs to be changed, whether it can be changed temporarily in order for the criminal intent to -- standard to be met. We cite the judgements of Appeal Courts -- Appeal Chambers, where it is clear that an ethnic map of a certain area has to be changed if we want to show that certain events took place with the intent of ethnic cleansing. We are completely in agreement with the position as expressed in the jurisprudence, that such changes need not be permanent, that such changes be temporary in nature in order to be able to find the existence of ethnic cleansing. In any case, this is something that is crucial to our position, and that is that an ethnic map has to be changed -- or ethnic balance has to be changed. The topic of forcible removal and ethnic cleansing is also something that is very important in this case. We wanted to point out that under the Geneva Conventions there is a difference between individual and en masse forcible removal, i.e., deportation. According to the Statute of this Tribunal, unlawful deportation or transfer pertains to civilians. The term of "ethnic cleansing" is a colloquial one rather than legal; it pertains to the creation of an ethnically homogeneous area. Through the commission of crime of deportation or forcible removal of one, two, three, or a dozen people in a certain area, does not appear to be en masse deportation or en masse forcible removal. Therefore, the crime of ethnic cleansing cannot be established. In other words, individual crimes of deportation can appear in a certain area as well as that of transfer without the existence of ethnic cleansing. In that case, it is unfounded to see those crimes as something that was committed with the intent to ethnically cleanse the territory in question. Your Honours, we will attempt to explain our position of the evidence and judgement based on only one single common criminal plan of ethnic cleansing. These are the five topics we wanted to tackle in this part of the presentation. Should you receive [as interpreted] additional clarifications on any of the issues, do interrupt me. As part of the first topic, we wanted to show in what way the majority modified the Prosecution's case. The Prosecutor submitted its indictment with 26 crimes with numerous locations and thousands of individual crimes under all existing types of liability. At the end of the case, having led all the witnesses, the Prosecutors formulated their case in their final brief. Based on all evidence presented, the Prosecutor stated what, in his view, was the criminal plan, what crimes were encompassed by that plan as part of JCE 1, and what crimes were seen as a foreseeable consequence, or JCE 3. The Chamber completely ignored this Prosecution case and the crimes defined as such, creating their own JCE case. We wanted to show this by the example of the crime of murder. Let us look at the next slide and then we can go back to this one. This is a brief analysis of all the crimes under the indictment, whereby we attempted to do the following as precisely as we could. We tried to see how many paragraphs were connected to particular crimes by the Prosecution, and at a first glance, it appears to be the case of detainment, conditions in detention centres, and the treatment of detainees. Over 50 per cent of all crimes pertained to this particular crime. Let us look at the crime of murder. It amounts to only 7 per cent of the overall amount of crimes encompassed by the indictment. There are no charges brought forth for attacking undefended villages or towns. If we analyse the evidence, we can see that in even the smallest location where there was fighting, there was resistance and that these were not attacks on civilians. The next slide, please. Your Honours, here we tried to show how the majority decided on the crime of murder, that is to say, under charges 2 and 3 of the indictment. In the first line, the first column, we can see how the Prosecutor presented it and we have all the locations here involving the crime of murder. We checked all the paragraphs in our -- in the indictment and, indeed, the paragraphs mentioned refer to the crime of murder. Let us look at how the Chamber made its findings about the responsibility for the crime of murder. They established that in terms of three locations the crime of murder pertained to JCE 1, and for the other location it is involves JCE 3. So three locations JCE 1; and the remaining locations, JCE 3. In the -- this is what we can find in the legal analysis part of the judgement. Although in one of the paragraphs, the Trial Chamber stated that all of the crimes of murder fall under category of JCE 1. There seems to be some kind of disorder there. It is impossible to establish a logical link, it seem, in the reasoning of the Chamber. If we take a look at which of the accused have been sentenced for that particular crime, as we can see in volume 4, and we have the crimes enumerated there under the two types of liability, if you do that, you will encounter a paradoxical fact. For the crimes of murder committed in the municipalities of Prozor and Jablanica, it was only Jadranko Prlic who was sentenced, the president of the civilian component of the HVO. If you compare that finding with the factual findings in the judgement, you will not come across a single logical or factual link. If we look at the crimes committed at the Heliodrom and the verdict pertaining to Bruno Stojic, you can see that he was found guilty under JCE 1 as well as JCE 3; whereas for other locations, no one was pronounce the guilty. And we believe the accused should be accused -- acquitted in that case. You can see from what I've presented so far that it is impossible to establish a link between the factual findings about the events in the field with regard to specific accused and the Trial Chamber's decision on sentencing. Let us go back to our slide number 12. If we take the example of this single crime, we can see that the final brief of the OTP defines which crimes are considered core crimes, amounting to JCE 1, as crimes that were committed as a foreseeable consequence connected to the events of the 30th of June, 1993. Irrespective of the fact that the Prosecution is our adversary, we believe we can fairly say that they invested maximum effort in drafting this part of the indictment based on the evidence they possessed, and I shared this thought with my learned friend, Mr. Stringer. The Trial Chamber completely ignored their definition of the case and established their own. Everything I said concerning the crime of murder applies to the crimes enumerated here. We are speaking about 12 crimes in total, crimes from Counts 21, 10, 11, 12 to 14, 15 to 17, and 18. The Trial Chamber pronounced its verdict contrary to the case as presented by the OTP in their final brief. In that sense, I fully endorse the position of the Prosecution when they stated that does not impact on the right accused to a fair trial, in the sense that they were informed in a timely fashion of the counts of their indictment because the indictment did cover all the possible time modalities and types of liability. However, we are of the view that the Trial Chamber erred in law in a different way. It went beyond the framework of the indictment. It is seen as impermissible in criminal law in our country and all the encounters of the former Yugoslavia as well as elsewhere. These are sufficient grounds to vacate a judgement. Let us look at slide 14 next and the topic of ethnic cleansing. In the left column, Your Honours, we presented quotes or extracts regarding the definition of ethnic cleansing as defined by the majority in their judgement. I also provided a reference, paragraphs 41 to 44 of volume 4 and 65 and 68. As you can see in the text, the Trial Chamber stated that there was a single common criminal purpose; and in order to further that plan, use was made of the political and military apparatus, that there was political purpose in order to further the plan as of mid-January, and that many crimes were committed. Only in a single paragraph, as defined in the following way, it is stated that these are crimes that fall within the framework of the common plan. This is how the majority defined the criminal plan or criminal purpose of ethnic cleansing. A criminal plan defined in that way is defined incorrectly and it invalidates the judgement. In the right column, we attempted a brief comparison with the position of the Trial Chambers in other cases, the cases being Tadic, Djordjevic, and Brdjanin. If the purpose is not criminal in and of itself, one needs to define the criminal means used or intended to further that plan as well. The next slide presents our basic thesis. We wanted to try to simply it as much as possible. Our first thesis is that there was no common criminal plan of ethnic cleansing of Muslim population. The second thesis is that until June 1993, there were no changes of the ethnic balance or map in any areas of Herceg-Bosna, and we intend to prove that. Our third thesis is that on the 30th of June, 1993, it wasn't the authorities of Herceg-Bosna that intended to implement their criminal plan of ethnic cleansing unprovoked, as stated by the majority. On that day, certain events took place. The HVO lost territory - without me going into any further detail because we intend to expand on this topic later on. I just briefly wanted to say that day, urgent security measures needed to be taken because there was a very true danger of HVO losing control over the entire territory of the Mostar region. Just a few words about the alleged necessity of ethnic cleansing. In my view, this is a key topic in the judgement and I want to devote quite some time to it. Unfortunately, the Chamber did not directly say that ethnic cleansing was a prerequisite for Bosnia-Herzegovina to be organised as a complex state in which one or several entities would have a majority Croat population. Why do I say "unfortunately"? Because, by failing to formulate this directly, the Chamber deprived us of the possibility to express our view on this claim. However, this claim is implicit in the entire judgement; it is implicit, especially in paragraph 41 of volume 4 that we will discuss a bit later. This implication is simply not correct. Herceg-Bosna was established towards the end of 1991. The Chamber did not find that the establishment of Herceg-Bosna was a -- marked the beginning of the crime of ethnic cleansing, and it is exceptionally important to bear in mind that Bosnia-Herzegovina under all plans made by the international community were supposed to be organised as a complex state in which one or more territorial units would have a majority Croat population. That was the case with the Cutileiro Plan from March 1992, that was the case with the Vance-Owen Plan from January 1993, and it was equally the case under the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan from August 1993. Not then and not later did anyone believe that organising Bosnia-Herzegovina as a complex state, a Federation, a confederation or any other form necessarily implies any ethnic cleansing. To believe that representatives of the international community created the maps that we will see later during this presentation implied ethnic cleansing in one of the territories are -- is simply unreasonable. We don't believe that a single reasonable trier of fact could conclude that any work in favour of organising Bosnia-Herzegovina as a complex state implied ethnic cleansing. Let us take a look at how the Trial Chamber analyses evidence and grounds its thesis on ethnic cleansing. That's paragraph 41. We will present this analysis in the following way. In one column, we present the findings from the judgement. The next column contains the evidence on which it is based. And then in the right-most column, we present our views in blue. The majority of the Trial Chamber made findings in paragraph 41, volume 4, that there was only one single criminal purpose, that is to say, domination of Croats through ethnic cleansing of the Muslim population. There is no footnote or any piece of evidence for this finding. In the next paragraph, the Chamber says, We will now present the reasons. Let us see how it did that. In paragraph 43 - as we've heard several times in this courtroom - the majority says that the leaders of Herceg-Bosna believed that to achieve the political purpose in the long-term, it was necessary to change the ethnic makeup of the territories claimed to form part of the HR HB. That is based on P89 and P21. The first piece of evidence is a transcript, that is to say, minutes of the meeting of 27 December 1991. Let me say just briefly. There is not a single word about ethnic cleansing in those minutes. The second document is a book by a relatively unknown author, Anto Valenta, which also does not contain a single word about ethnic cleansing. Therefore, Your Honours, we believe that this finding of the majority does not only fail to be the only reasonable but totally impossible. We believe that not a single reasonable trier of fact could have concluded that any of the leaders of Herceg-Bosna thought ethnic cleansing was necessary. The judgement says that from October 1991, Prlic, Stojic, Petkovic, and Praljak were aware that the implementation of the purpose of -- would involve the Muslim population moving outside. That is based on P11380. However, neither in the factual findings nor in this document do we find a single word about ethnic cleansing. Now let us look at paragraph 44, where the Chamber notes that in mid-January 1993 the leaders of Herceg-Bosna decided to proceed with the plan of ethnically cleansing the Muslims. In the next column, we show the documents from the footnote on which the Chamber bases this finding. We analysed all this evidence thoroughly and we can say briefly. The evidence pertaining to that time-period do not contain a single word about ethnic cleansing, and the rest of the documents do not pertain to January 1993 at all, nor do they speak to any events of ethnic cleansing in the Gornji Vakuf area. Based on this evidence, in our view, not a single reasonable trier of fact could find that there was a criminal plan to move out the Muslim population beginning in mid-January 1993. If we continue analysing the judgement in relation to Gornji Vakuf, that's paragraphs 45 and 48 of volume 4, we will see that there was no ethnic cleansing in Gornji Vakuf at all. There were no incidents that could be even remotely considered as ethnic cleansing. The HVO indeed attacked four villages. Those four villages were defended. And the Chamber concluded - I'm not going to read everything in this slide - but the Chamber found that a number, I emphasise a number of civilians, were moved from Hrasnica and Dusa. Some civilians were moved from Hrasnica and Dusa. We cite a document from the BH army, P1226, in which the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina discusses an evacuation of population from Hrasnica and Uzricje. We will deal more with this later. Let us look at this table. This is Gornji Vakuf, the 1991 census. You can see these four villages with their total population, with their ethnic makeup; but what we wish to demonstrate with this slide is that there were 50 settlements in the Gornji Vakuf municipalities. So HVO did attack these four populated areas, but evacuating a few Muslims from a few villages certainly does not amount to ethnic cleansing. In this slide, we wanted to provide a simple summary of what we've just said. Several civilians moved from Hrasnica to -- and Uzricje and Bugojno, that is to say, another municipality, and they were escorted by the UNPROFOR. All the other residents remained in the Gornji Vakuf municipalities. These are our conclusions concerning Gornji Vakuf and we believe they are the only reasonable conclusions possible. In January 1993, the ethnic map of the municipality was not changed. Not a single reasonable trier of fact could have come to the conclusion that the HVO military actions in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993 were launched to further the common criminal plan of ethnic cleansing of Muslim population; and therefore, the Petkovic's conviction for crimes committed in this municipality in January 1993 under the JCE form 3 should simply be invalidated. Now, one remark that we believe is especially important for a correct understanding of the events on the ground. Your Honours, from late January to mid-April 1993, there is not a single charge in the indictment, so nothing is happening at this time. The Prosecutor believes that the criminal plan of ethnic cleansing of Muslims was created in January, but at this time - apart from the incident in four relatively small villages - nothing happened in January 1993. This fact alone is sufficient proof that at that time there was no criminal plan of ethnic cleansing of the Muslim population. Now let us look at Jablanica in April 1993. The Chamber states itself here in paragraph 46 that there were tensions in this period up to mid-April -- let me just note that there is no such claim in the indictment. In mid-April, indeed, a conflict broke out, and we will analyse these connects further. HVO, indeed, attacked Sovici and Doljani villages. Certain crimes were, indeed, committed there. The Trial Chamber established there were skirmishes and fighting and HVO activity in these villages was partly defensive. But what is of import to us in view of the criminal plan defined as it was is the claim that this particular number of civilians was deported from Jablanica municipality, 450 civilians. This simply incorrect. In paragraph 613, volume 2, the Chamber held that it had no sufficient evidence as to what happened with the civilians from Sovici who were initially indeed taken away from Jablanica municipality and into the Gornji Vakuf municipality. This is not true. There is evidence in the case file that clearly shows that these civilians arrived at Jablanica in the beginning of June 1993. Just a few crucial facts as to what really happened. In early May 1993, this area was visited by commanders of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and senior officers of the HVO, including Petkovic; the civilians in Sovici, together with ABiH commanders, discussed whether to stay or to go. They expressed their wish to leave Sovici, whereas Halilovic and Pasalic requested from the HVO that they secure buses, and the HVO obliged. However, due to obstacles on the road, the buses were not able to go to Jablanica; instead, they turned to Gornji Vakuf. However, several weeks later, these civilians nevertheless arrived at Jablanica. Here is the census of Jablanica from 1991. We show all the settlements in Jablanica. You can see from these figures that Doljani was a majority-Croat village; Sovici, a majority-Muslim village. The next slide, according to the same methodology as Gornji Vakuf, we display this data and evidence. In the right column, you will see the exhibits for this allegation that I made, this assertion that I made, that the civilians remained in Jablanica. It's P2825. Witness CA, transcript 10042, transcript 10311. And there were also Defence witnesses who discussed this, but I will deal with that in my response, if necessary. And the conclusion for Jablanica. The ethnic map of Jablanica has not been changed after the events of mid-April 1993. All the civilians from this municipality remained there. Therefore, no reasonable trier of fact could have concluded that the HVO military actions in that period were launched to the further criminal plan of ethnic cleansing of the Muslim population; and therefore, Petkovic's conviction for crimes in the municipality of Jablanica in April 1993 under the JCE form of liability should be vacated. The next municipality, Your Honours, is Prozor. We show in a simple manner here that the Chamber itself says that there was no ethnic cleansing in Prozor. There were no deportations or transfers. The Chamber held that up to the end of August 1993 Muslims remained in their hometowns and villages, and that's when the expulsion of Muslims began. The conclusion for Prozor, April 1993, there are no charges for the crimes of deportation or forcible transfer. Muslims were not removed from Prozor, the ethnic map was not changed, and no reasonable trier of fact could consequently have come to the conclusion that any crimes were committed at that time to further the common criminal plan of ethnic cleansing. Accordingly, Petkovic's conviction for crimes in Prozor under the JCE form of liability should be invalidated. Now let us move to Mostar, which is a bit more complicated but still quite simple, in April and May. In this slide, Your Honour, we are displaying the key thesis of the Trial Chamber for this period in Mostar. We wish to emphasise paragraph 50, where the Chamber notes that Muslim refugees from Central Bosnia are arriving in Mostar. We wish to point out that this claim about the arrival of Muslim refugees from Central Bosnia continuously throughout this period simply contradicts the fact that in January 1993 a criminal plan was formed to ethnically cleanse the Muslims. We also wish to point out the assertions from paragraph 53 but not only all the paragraphs pertaining to the arrival of Croats from Central Bosnia simultaneously with the Muslims; all of theme were fleeing primarily because fighting with Serbian army and later of an outbreak of an open conflict between Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO, Croats flee from the areas conquered by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There's one particular incident we wish to underline because the Trial Chamber made an inaccurate finding. There is no ethnic cleansing in this period. As the Trial Chamber correctly held, there was no expulsion of Muslims in May -- there were expulsions in 1993. This claim is completely incorrect. It would take a lot of time to explain why, but we dealt with it in our brief in paragraphs -- regrettably we did not write the judgement but all right. So in paragraphs 63 to 67. To finish with Mostar, in April and May 1993, Muslim refugees are arriving in Mostar. For April 1993, no crimes are charged in the indictment. The ethnic map of Mostar in that period is not changed in favour of Croats or to the detriment of Muslims. No reasonable trier of fact, we believe, could have come to the conclusion that the events in Mostar were a consequence of any intent to implement a plan of ethnic cleansing. Therefore, we believe that Petkovic's conviction for crimes in Mostar in this period under the JCE should be vacated. For the brief period October 1993 in Stupni Do, we, Your Honours, do not find fault with any finding about the crimes established, but we wish to say that the Prosecution does not charge any crimes of deportation or forcible transfer, and the Trial Chamber did not find that any military actions were launched for the purpose of ethnically cleansing the Muslims from that area. And therefore, we believe that no reasonable trier of fact could conclude that the crimes in Stupni Do were committed to further the common criminal plan of ethnic cleansing of Muslim population. Accordingly, Petkovic's conviction for crimes committed in Stupni Do in that period under the JCE should be reversed. I also wish to emphasise that the Prosecutor himself regarding these allegations states that there was no ethnic cleansing and liability should be considered under other forms of liability envisaged by the Statute. And to conclude about the ethnic cleansing. So, in Gornji Vakuf, in January 1993, the Muslim population was not removed. In Jablanica in April 1993, neither. Neither in Prozor in April 1993. And in Mostar until June 1993, quite indubitably and unequivocally there were no deportations. The same goes for Vares and Stupni Do. Therefore, we believe, Your Honours, that for all the crimes in this period in these locations, there are no grounds for conviction under JCE. Your Honours, now we come to the topic of the 30th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel, could you enlighten the Appeals Chamber as to whether these documents in which you tried to show that there were no demographic changes in certain localities, have these documents been presented to the Trial Chamber? And, secondly, could you tell us what is the source in terms of official data on which you base yourself in producing these charts?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hope that what I'm going to -- that this reply now will not be taking away from my time of two hours. So I can reply briefly [In English] Just to know to be brief or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We don't have several types of accounting. Judges are entitled to ask you questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Your Honours, we did not discuss the criminal plan of ethnic cleansing in the hearing as the only criminal plan, as the key substance of JCE. The indictment was created in the way that all 26 crimes were all under the JCE mode of responsibility. We dealt more can facts, who was moved out, where, what was happening in specific municipalities; but the topic of ethnic cleansing as the only objective of the criminal intent, as the core crime, was actually not a topic of discussion. And this is what I stated. In the judgement, by creating the JCE in such a way, the Trial Chamber completely changed the case that we were actually presenting before this Tribunal. As for evidence, all the exhibits that I referred to here are cited mostly in the judgement. Most of the exhibits that I referred to are from the Prosecution witnesses. And if you're asking about statistical data -- I apologise, Your Honours, are you interested in learning whether statistical data is derived from or which data that I'm referring to here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure, counsel, that are you -- the materials that you are citing are based on some kind of official data.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yeah. [Interpretation] All that I have been saying is based on documents that are in the case file, except for the tables which actually are analysis of the judgement that I created. All other documents are documents that are exhibits in this case. As for the statistical data, that is data from the population census of 1991, but I think that that is not something that is in dispute. [In English] If I may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We come to the topic of the 30th of June, 1993, when full-out war began between the BiH army and the HVO. Your Honours, you can look at what the Trial Chamber established happened on the 30th of June or up until that date. The Trial Chamber knows or knew that at that time the BiH launched an offensive. The Trial Chamber knew that Muslim soldiers of the HVO deserted from some units of the HVO and joined the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. The Trial Chamber knew that because of that betrayal, the HVO lost control over certain areas in the Mostar region. The Trial Chamber knew that the B&H army at that time intended to link up the Mostar area with the area of Konjic and Jablanica. The Trial Chamber knew that the HZ HB authorities took certain actions in response to the attack launched on the 30th of June, 1993. All these things were established in volume 2, paragraphs 878 to 885. Your Honours, we believe that already on the basis of these assertions each reasonable trier of fact would conclude from the evidence that measures undertaken on the 30th of June cannot represent the only consequence and understand that their only objective was to cleanse the Muslim population. We are going to show as we go on what was going on at the fronts in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the start, could you please look at what the Prosecutor stated in the Hadzihasanovic indictment. We're already seen that in the courtroom over the past couple of days, but I feel it's all right to remind you of that. The Prosecutor states that from the April -- April 1993 and early summer 1993, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina carried out a series of attacks against the HVO including - but not limiting itself to - the municipalities and then they list the municipalities: Bugojno, Busovaca, Maglaj, Novi Travnik, Travnik, Vares, Vitez, Kakanj, and so on and so forth. The Prosecution asserts that those operations by the armija culminated in a massive attack in June 1993 at Kakanj, Travnik, and Zenica, among others. These assertions by the Prosecution are absolutely accurate. We will show documents in support of that. All these documents -- I'm not going to have enough time to cite all of them so that we could have them in the transcript, but all these documents can be found in Annex I of the Petkovic appeal brief. A document at the end of March 1993, 4D438, it's a document by the BiH army, speaks about the events in Konjic. Your Honours, in mid-April 1993, Konjic is the key to all subsequent events. In early April, HVO report, P1083 -- 1803 about the attacks on the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. Reports by the armija about its own activities -- excuse me, I cited the wrong document. It's a HVO document confirming combat actions by the Bosnia and Herzegovina army, 2D774. Then we have a series of documents from early April and then from mid-April, where you can see what was going on in Konjic and the surrounding area. We're going to stay on slide 38 a little bit longer. We need to keep this slide confidential. There is a protected document, so I kindly ask that the slide not be broadcast outside of the courtroom. May I continue, Your Honours? I would like to draw your attention, in particular, Your Honours, to a document in the upper left-hand corner, 4D599. This is a report by the BiH army of the 17th of April, 1993, and we can see here the operations that are being carried out and the conclusion at the end. We will try to have the work in Konjic completed as soon as possible and then start with all brigades counter attacks in two directions. The first towards Jablanica and Mostar; and the second towards Prozor and Rama. We're going to speak specifically about these initial activities under 1 towards Jablanica and Mostar. Your Honours, you can see in all of these documents that the BiH army in mid-April 1993 launched operations to capture areas that, up until then, were under the control of the HVO. We draw your attention to a protected document in the lower right-hand corner which states that the B&H army managed to push the HVO out of many areas and it seems that the Croat population was fleeing from those areas. This is a report from the 14th of June, 1993. The next document, we will now look at slide 39. That is also a protected document, protected slide. The document in the upper right-hand corner is a report about how, on 13th of June, the B&H army captured Kakanj, and we can also see that the B&H army offensive continues. We are showing a speech by Arif Pasalic here of the 30th of June, 1993. This is document 2D448. This speech was also referred to my learned friend Mr. Karnavas in his submissions. On that day, the commander of the BiH army calls on all citizens that can carry a pistol or a stone to begin killing criminal Ustashas, and so on and so forth. There is a report of the 1st of July, 1993. It's in the lower left-hand corner, 2D1389, and we can see the areas that were captured by the Army of BiH, not just the Tihomir Misic barracks, Your Honour, as this is a simplified conclusion by the majority but actually the entire northern area, north of Mostar, and could you please look at the concluding sentence which states: "According to a report by the 4th Corps, the units of this corps linked up with the forces of the 6th Corps, which will have a positive effect on the coming combat operations." The 4th was in Jablanica and the 6th Corps was in Mostar. Oh, I'm being corrected by the Generals, actually it's the other way around as far as the corps locations are concerned. Just a brief explanation about this so on our next slide, slide 40, and now we can go back to open session. The HVO, of course, has information about what is going on in the ground, in the field. At the time General Petkovic, in late June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We might -- you might have given the impression that we were in private session, but somehow we were transmitting just the same to the public. That's not the case. What we were not transmitting are two documents only, but otherwise we were in open session and we are still in open session. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your clarification. In late June 1993, Petkovic was trying to inform representatives of the international community -- this is slide 40. Slide 40. We cannot see the slides on our screen. Oh, everyone else has them but we don't. In any event, in late June, General Petkovic was trying to inform General Morillon and other representatives of the international community and ask them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I -- one moment. Can I ask for technical assistance to the Defence, please. In the meantime, you can proceed. It's your own document, so you know it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is all right now; we have it on the screen. This is document 4D702, and we gave you a short excerpt from the testimony of General Petkovic and Mr. Radmilo Jasak. I wanted to draw your attention to the words of General Petkovic: "I did not even think that everything would happen in that form and manner." This is transcript 49585. The following slide, slide 41, it's just a brief reminder about the events after the 30th of June. In July 1993, the BiH army captured Kostajnica, yes, Kostajnica, which was a Croat enclave in the Konjic municipality; then Fojnica; then Bugojno; then Doljani. I would like to remind, Your Honours, that Doljani is the same place, the same village, that we spoke about in relation to April 1993. In October 1993, the BiH army captured some locations in the Vares municipality. And in November 1993, the ABiH enters Vares. Could we now look at maps? Can we look at a representation of what was going on. So the first map in the upper left-hand corner shows Central Bosnia in January 1993. HVO-control territories are in blue; and territory under control of the B&H army is in green. When you look at these four maps, you can see right away that by -- mid-1993, the area under the control of the B&H army is becoming larger. I'm going to repeat what happened month by month, but this is really all -- evident when you look at these maps. The next slide is what happened in Central Bosnia by the end of the year. And you can see at the end that in Central Bosnia, there are only two enclaves left. On the lower left-hand corner, you can see how many Croats from which municipality left after the B&H army captured that area. It's the map on the lower right-hand corner. What we said about Mostar, now we can also on the maps. We can see the map on the left in blue is territory under the control of the HVO; territory in green is BiH army. And then you look at the situation after the 30th of June, 1993. So on the 30th of June, 1993, the territory around Mostar was captured by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in co-operation with Muslim soldiers in the HVO. The next map of slide 45 shows us the Mostar, Jablanica, and Konjic area, that region. And can you see what the situation was on the 30th of June and what the situation was on the 30th of June. Could you please keep these maps in mind when we begin analysing the security measures that were adopted on the 30th of June and why the 30th of June is a turning point in the conflicts between the armija and the HVO. And now, briefly, I can summarise what I have just said. From April 1993, the BiH army continuously broadened territory under its control. Military actions of the BiH army are relevant as evidence that certain actions, activities, measures taken by the HVO authorities were in reaction to and the consequence of the ABiH offensive actions and plans, and not a criminal plan of ethnic cleansing of Muslim population. Therefore, we believe, Your Honours, that no reasonable trier of fact could have come to the conclusion that on the 30th of June, 1993 authorities of the Herceg-Bosna decided to implement the plan of ethnically cleansing the Muslims population without any provocation at all. Now we're going to deal with some protected documents, so I also kindly ask that these documents be not broadcast. There are numerous documents on this topic. We wanted to show you this issue through documents by representatives of the international community. Those representatives reported and noted that Muslim soldiers of the HVO deserted. They joined the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and because of that, the HVO - and perhaps the HVO, amongst other things - lost control of the area around Mostar. There was a danger that the HVO would completely lose control in the region of Mostar unless measures were taken. The next slide does not have any protected documents. There is some information, Your Honour, generally about Muslims in the HVO. Dr. Prlic's Defence spoke to you about how the HVO was the only multi-ethnic army in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. We absolutely support that assertion, and we're going to prove that, the same as Praljak and Stojic's Defence. The HVO was formed as a joint Army of Croats and Muslims who lived in the area of Herceg-Bosna. We would now like to show you from a series of documents that the Bosnia and Herzegovina army was continually in touch with Muslim soldiers of the HVO. These documents can be found as Annex 13 of Petkovic's final trial brief, without this first document that I'm nothing going to present to you. All of the previous Defence teams also pointed this out. We just wanted to remind you of the document 2D150; it is from June 1993. It was at the time of the fierce clashes between the ABiH and HVO. In the table, you can see the ethnic composition of the HVO brigades. Please look at the 1st Brigade: 35 per cent were Muslim; in the 2nd Brigade, nearly 21 per cent; in the 3rd, a bit over 13 per cent. Before this date, the number of Muslim soldiers was significantly higher. There were units with up to 50 per cent of Muslim soldiers in their ranks. The HVO was, indeed, created as a joint force of Croats and Muslims. While I am on this topic, I wanted to tell you why I refer to the term "Muslims" rather than "Bosniaks." It is simply because at the time I'm discussing the official title of the Bosniak people was Muslim, or Muslims. As for the rest of the documents here, you can see that the authorities of Herceg-Bosna believed that there might occur a security problem due to the high figures of Muslims in the HVO. However, nobody raised it as an issue, nor was it created into a problem. The Muslims were in no way discriminated, nor were they prevented from joining the HVO. We, in particular, wanted to point out the document 4D568 which is at the bottom right side dated the 16th of April, 1993. Have a look, Your Honours, at this quotation from April 1993. There is a possibility of an all-out war with the HVO and the need to establish contact with the Muslim soldiers so that at the right moment they could join the HVO --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an ABiH document testifying to the plans that the Muslim soldiers of the HVO at some point joined the ranks of the ABiH. The next slide shows a protected document. Here can you see 4D 33, also mid-April 1993. It reads: "Call upon all Muslim members of the HVO to place themselves on the side of their people ..." A document of the 18th of April, which is 4D34, reads as follows. It says: "... establish co-operation with our soldiers in the HVO and point out the seriousness of the situation to them ..." Let us move on. Another ABiH document, 4D35. There was a separate plan of informing the Muslim soldiers of the HVO in the units specified or in the units that were in the municipalities specified here. Document 4D473, it is an indirect threat to a HVO commander. It says: "I mention ... that a large number of Muslim soldiers are in your formations ..." The last document on the left is 4D36 dated the 2nd of May, 1993. An ABiH commander mentions what operations need to be undertaken and ordered a linkup with "our men in the HVO," specifying their tasks in Capljina. The last bullet point of the document reads: "Seize the town of Stolac with our people in the HVO." Let us conclude now with the 30th of June, 1993, Your Honours. As regards General Petkovic's order to isolate the Muslim soldiers of the HVO as well as Muslim military conscripts, all this needs to be viewed through the prism of events of the 30th of June, 1993. Hence, do bear in mind what took place on that day. The ABiH led offensive operations against the HVO and continuously broadened territory under its control. ABiH conquered territory north of Mostar, in co-operation with the HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity. Similarly, if such scenario happened in other HVO units, the HVO might lose control over entire territory. Immediate security measures had to be taken and they, indeed, were taken. Owing to those measures, the lines of confrontation in Mostar remained unchanged and nearly unchanged in the Mostar area, although the fighting lasted until April 1994. That is why we believe, Your Honours, that no reasonable trier of fact could conclude that the measures undertaken by the Herceg-Bosna authorities on the 30th of June, 1993, were -- they were -- not the consequence of something that was going on in the field. They were a direct result of it. In our view, no reasonable trier of fact could conclude that those measures were taken with the aim of implementing the criminal plan of ethnic cleansing of Muslim population. The conclusion of this part of our presentation is on the next slide. No reasonable trier of fact could have concluded that there was a common criminal plan of ethnic cleansing created in mid-January 1993. No reasonable trier of fact could have concluded that there were any changes to the demographics of the aforementioned municipalities until the 30th of June, the ABiH broadened the territory under its control. Due to all these events, no reasonable trier of fact could have come to the conclusion that, on that day, a decision was made to intensify and further the common criminal plan of ethnic cleansing. Let us now move on to Milivoj Petkovic himself while remaining still with the 30th of June. We will discuss his role through the eight topics presented here. The first one pertains to borders. BiH borders appear to be a very simple matter in the view of General Petkovic and his Defence. As early as April 1993, at a meeting General Petkovic told General Halilovic that Croatia simply cannot wish to change any BiH borders and annex part of its territory because, at that moment, there was Republika Srpska Krajina existing in its very territory that also wanted to secede from Croatia and join the territories controlled by the Bosnian Serbs as well as the territory of Serbia proper. If Croatia would favour annexing part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it would make the RSK request to secede legitimate. That is what General Petkovic said in 1993. He repeated the very same thing before this Tribunal. We see it as something so simple, that any scenario about the change of borders is unnecessary or uncalled for. As of the first moment of the breakup of former Yugoslavia, the conclusion was made that the former republics may acquire the status of states, but that no borders can be forcefully changed in any way. Hence, the story of the borders actually means shifting the focus away from the gist of the case. Let us see whether there could have existed any criminal intention on part of General Petkovic. Let us look at some attempts to establish a joint command for the ABiH and HVO. These documents can be found in Annex 2 of Petkovic's final trial brief. Your Honours, we see three slides here, this one and two more, specifying the documents, where we can see that in July 1992 until June 1993, there were continuous discussions, attempts, decisions to establish a joint command. The first such document is P339, agreement between Izetbegovic and Tudjman dated the 21st of July, 1992. In particular, we wanted to draw your attention to some documents from January 1993 at the time when allegedly the criminal plan of ethnic cleansing was designed. Let us look, therefore, at the last two documents on this slide, one dated the 27th of January, 1993, which is a joint statement by Izetbegovic and Boban, calling for the establishment of joint commands at all levels without delay. And then we have the order of Petkovic on the same day, which is P1322. The next slide also shows some documents from January, such as Arif Pasalic's order as well as an order by General Petkovic on the 28th of January. In February, you see similar attempts. You can see them take place in April as well, and we can see it on this slide in May as well. The last document pertaining to 1993 stems from June. These documents show that in June 1993 something happened which made any further discussion on co-operation between the ABiH and HVO impossible, at least not in the same way. The last document is from 1994, after the Washington Accords. Finally after that, a joint command of the ABiH and HVO was established. The next topic is very important to us, Your Honours. We wanted to point out some documents showing that the HVO believed throughout that the ABiH is an ally, at least the 30th of June 1993. First we look at Herbert Okun's note, P1038. He was very tidy in terms of keeping notes from meetings. This one comes from Geneva on the 2nd of January during peace negotiations. He noted that Halilovic and Petkovic agreed to establish joint command of the BiH army and the HVO and that Mladic said that the alliance of Croatia and Alija Izetbegovic against the Serb people should cease to exist. The majority concluded that this was the period when the JCE was created. As a matter of fact, it is during this time that attempts were made to create a joint command and establish co-operation. Let us look at what kind of instruction Petkovic issued to his units, 4D397, from June 1992. Petkovic warned that they are a common armed force, that clashes should be avoided, and that the common enemy should be fought instead of fighting each other. On the next slide, we see a number of documents. However, given the amount of time I have, I will only focus on the last document on the bottom right. The document is dated the 11th of January, 1993; it is an order by Milivoje Petkovic, 4D354. He referred to the ABiH as "our allies." The next slide, the 13th January, 1993, P1115. Petkovic ordered that contact should be established immediately with the Muslim side and problems solved through talks. On the 11th of January, 1993, Petkovic addressed the units in the towns mentioned, P1190. He stated: "We do not want the problems with the Muslims as -- to escalate again ..." The 20th of January 1993, 4D433. Again, Petkovic ordered to Konjic that contact should be established with the BiH army. The 27th of January, 1993, 4D19. Again, Petkovic ordered that all disputes be dealt with through negotiations. The same goes for February 1993. In particular, I want to draw your attention to the bottom right document, 4D75. Petkovic wrote to Halilovic on the 9th of February, 1993, saying: "I looked forward to each new soldier, Croatian or Muslim, because I knew that they had a common goal." Let us look at the next slide. I'd like to draw your attention to the last document. Again, Petkovic's order to all operational zones, P2599. As late as June 1993, Petkovic wrote: "You should negotiate with the Muslim side to calm the situation whenever it is possible." Your Honours, in the next few slides, we'll show you a number of documents as contained in Annex I of Petkovic's final trial brief. There are quite many of them. These documents prove that the HVO and ABiH were equal components of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, to see the HVO as an illegal or unlawful paramilitary armed force is completely incorrect and unfounded. The 21st of July, 1992, Izetbegovic and Tudjman agreement - we've already referred to it - it refers to the HVO as an integral component of the armed forces of the Republic of BiH. The next slide. We see a number of documents, including certain statements an orders by Alija Izetbegovic, where the HVO is seen as a component of the armed forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. A few documents need taking note of. P2002 of the 20th of April, 1993. Halilovic and Petkovic signed an agreement establishing that the ABiH and the HVO are equal. On the 25th of April, 1993, we see something very similar in two documents. One was a joint statement by Boban, Izetbegovic, and Tudjman. It is P2078; the other, an annex to the statement referring to the Halilovic-Petkovic agreement, P2091. The next slide we see that HVO is still treated as a legitimate armed force. Finally, in the Washington Agreement, which is 4D1234, we see the HVO defined as part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Afterwards, follow excerpts from the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina showing that the HVO was an equitable component and that service in the HVO counted towards pensionable years of service. Then we see part of Petkovic's movement in 1991 that we took from the case file. From this, we see that in January 1993, Petkovic spent about half a month in Geneva at peace talks, and we see also that in that month he also held negotiations with commanders of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If we look at April and May 1993, you will see that Petkovic spent most of that time at negotiations touring the field together with Halilovic and other ABH senior officers, attempting to resolve conflicts by negotiations, talks, and peace agreements. In one interview that we see on the next slide, at that time in February 1993, and that's 4D100, he stated that demilitarisation of the state is the only solution because as long as there are so many troops in that area, conflicts are inevitable. We especially want to draw your attention to one interview Petkovic gave in August 1994, 4D1355. At that time, during the war he said: "We never prepared for a war with Muslims. We never wanted to start conflicts anywhere else." Petkovic repeated that before this Court on transcript page 49414. He said then and now that his position was: "It's better to negotiate for two years than wage war for one single day." We will now show you an excerpt from an interview in 1993 where --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "It is better to try to achieve political agreement for one or two years than wage war for one single day. I believe it's time for war to stop in this part of the world. It's better to negotiate for a year or two even than wage war for five months or even one day."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's all we wanted to show you in this context. On slide 68, we wish to show you that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in June conquered Travnik and Kakanj and in court Petkovic said in this connection: "Only then did I definitively realise there is no longer any certain hope of stopping these events through negotiations." Transcript 49458. Just a few words now about a document that is a key document in this case, that's Petkovic's order from 1993, 30th of June, 1993, issued to up with operative zone of the HVO, not the entire HVO - which is exceptionally important if we talk about security reasons. That's P3019. Let us look at his exact words. He ordered that Muslim soldiers of the HVO be disarmed an isolated. He used the word "isolate," that's what I wish to emphasise, and he also ordered the isolation of all able-bodied men in Muslim-inhabited villages. It's very important to bear in mind that he ordered that civilians should not be touched, that civilians must remain in their homes. We have elaborated this in our brief and in our submissions until now. He followed the orders of the Supreme Commander of the HVO, Mate Boban. These orders were publicly known; they were notified to representatives of the international community. There was no secret about this. There was no concealment. There was no criminal intent. We will now show you a slide with a protected statement. This is an excerpt from the opinion of two military experts we've heard before the Court. One is a Defence expert, Milan Gorjanc, and another is a Prosecution expert, Andrew Pringle. They talk about the same thing, the statements of Muslim soldiers, the danger of losing territory in the entire Mostar region, betrayals by Muslim soldiers, et cetera. And it was very important to make the decision about disarming and isolating Muslim soldiers. To conclude about the disarmament and isolation of Muslim soldiers, let us repeat. We think this decision was justified, for several reasons. First of all, a significant number of Muslims deserted from the HVO and joined the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Second, the ABH, as result of their betrayal, broadened control in parts of the Mostar region. And, third, the HVO was in a position of potentially losing control over the whole Mostar region. Based on these premises, it is indubitable that special security measures were called for. Petkovic's order was legal. One, it was issued upon the order of the HVO Supreme Commander. Two, the decision was made to disarm and isolate one's own soldiers, and the time they spent in detention centres was recognised later as time spent in a military unit and was recorded as special double length of service for retirement purposes, as if they had been involved in fighting. Document 4D1466. And the next reason is: There is no law that prohibits an army to isolate -- from isolating or detaining its own soldiers. We wish to point out, Your Honours, that almost all Defence teams put forward the argument that the international humanitarian law does not apply to measures that an army applies to its own troops. The Trial Chamber regrettably failed to respond to these positions and arguments and found an alternative solution by treating these men as not belonging to any army. We believe it's not only erroneous but also contrary to common sense, to treat Muslim soldiers of the HVO as men who did not belong to any army because at that time those were soldiers of the HVO. Just a few words about another important element and that's the isolation of able-bodied Muslim men of military age. This is an excerpt from the commentary to Geneva Conventions and parts of the judgement in the Kordic case. In our view, it transpires quite clearly and indubitably that military-age able-bodied men are not a priori civilians and there is a perfectly good security reason to detain such men, in order to establish first whether they are civilians or not. Let me emphasise that if the status of civilian was part of the features of a crime then the Prosecutor needs to establish that status for every person the Prosecutor claims to be a civilian. So it's completely erroneous to identify a whole group of people as civilians or not, especially -- unless it is a group of women, children, and the elderly. And it is necessary to establish whether a military-age able-bodied man is a civilian or not. He is not a civilian a priori. We also wish to point out the finding in Kordic, where in view of the fact that both of ABH and HVO operated on the principle of stints or shifts, which meant that they were on the front line some time and then spent some time at home; and they remained soldiers even while at home, with their weapons. That's why we believe, Your Honours, that the decision of General Petkovic to isolate military-age able-bodied men should be detained is legal and justified. It's justified because at the time the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as we said, was conducting offensive operations against the HVO and able-bodied military-age men were physically capable and legally duty-bound to join the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that constituted a security risk for the HVO. Isolating military-age able-bodied Muslim men was legal because there is no law that prohibits it because, as I've said, they cannot be presumed to be civilians. That, of course, doesn't know -- doesn't mean that they should be kept detained, detained without establishing their specific circumstances. It needs to be established whether they are, indeed, civilians or not; and if they are civilians, it needs to be further established whether they constitute a security risk or not. And if they are civilians and if they are no security risk, they must be released. These men, military-age able-bodied men, if they are detained, must have the status of prisoner of war because they were military conscripts of the BH army and, as such, they were reserve troops of the BH army. We elaborated on that in our appeal brief and for shortage of time, I'm skipping this section. Just one more thing. In keeping with the finding in Kordic of the Appeals Chamber, this decision ask not discriminatory in nature because it does not apply to the entire Muslim population but only one of its segments, that is to say, military-age able-bodied men who are not to be presumed to be civilians and who could be a security threat. In that sense, we believe we should make a distinction between initial detention and decision-making on continued detention. Petkovic absolutely assumes his part of responsibility for the initial detention of Muslim able-bodied military-age men and his own decision of the 30th of June, 1993. His position is that this detention was both legal and justified. He, however, was not qualified to decide whether they were indeed civilians and whether they should remain in detention or not. That is why I am concluding this passage on detention here. In July 1993, Petkovic requested to be relieved of duty of the chief of the HVO Main Staff and the reason is very simple. What he had been doing up to then - and that is trying to solve problems through negotiation - was no longer a way to solve problems with the BH army. He returns to the position of the chief of HVO staff after the Washington Agreements, that is to say, in early 1994. And in this context, we wish to underline that nobody from the Muslim side or from the international community had any objection to his return to that position. And to conclude, we believe that the majority completely unreasonably concluded that Petkovic acted with the intent of expelling the Muslim population from Herceg-Bosna. We believe that this is certainly not the only possible reasonable conclusion from the evidence, and Petkovic's conviction under the JCE form of criminal responsibility should be overturned. And if I'm correct, I still have eight minutes left and I will -- I would like to use these eight minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are indeed correct. You have eight minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In these eight minutes, we will respond to the questions you put without repeating what other Defence teams have said so far, although we subscribe to everything they've said, including the written submission of the Bruno Stojic Defence. We will add three things: Gornji Vakuf, occupation, and terror against civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correction: There is no written submission that I know of, unless you are referring to the brief. What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I refer to the skeleton they provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may think it is a brief, but it's not a brief. I made it clear that it's not part of the records.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] But if anybody happens to read what's written there, we agree, for the record. You put the question, Your Honours, about the report by Siljeg. The document is 13 -- just a moment, 1351, P1351. We wish to show you the context, Your Honours, because we are certain that this context will enable you to understand better the import of this report. And just a short point before that. The first one is a letter from Arif Pasalic to Halilovic from 19 January 1993, where he says that they met with some people, including my client, General Petkovic, and agreed on a cease-fire in Gornji Vakuf. On the same day, the same order on a cease-fire is issued by Mate Boban, P1211. Mate Boban is the chief commander of the HVO. The next slide. On the next day, 20th January 1993, Petkovic and Pasalic issued a joint order on a cease-fire. The document is P1238. We draw your attention to point 3 and that is: "Set up a commission consisting of three members from the HVO and the BH army each to monitor the carrying out of this Order and solve the disputed issues on the ground with the assistance of UNPROFOR and the ECMM." So it's the 20th of January, 1993, the time when the Trial Chamber claims the criminal plan of -- for ethnic cleansing was conceived. On the 20th of January, fire ceased. On the 24th of January, in Geneva when they found out that fighting did not cease based on this order, Petkovic issued a new order for a cease-fire, P1286. After that, Siljeg on the 25th of January issues an order to respect the cease-fire absolutely, and that's P1300. That's when the fighting, indeed, ceased. Then we have a joint statement from 27 January 1993 by Izetbegovic -- by Petkovic and Siljeg. And on 28th of January, an order by Petkovic and Arif Pasalic, another order. This is a report by Siljeg, and my colleague pointed out that this report covers what the fact-finding commission established in villages where fighting had taken place. Based on that report, which my client did receive, he issued instructions in P1344: "Arrest and imprison all our extremists." In the same order, he also made an order in point 7: "... arrest looters on our side ..." This is a document which attempted to establish the consequences of warfare in these villages and a record of how many people in these villages wished to leave and expressed this wish to the UNPROFOR. You see exactly what we said at the beginning. Only a few people from a few villages left Gornji Vakuf; the rest remained in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf. We believe this document by Zeljko Siljeg demonstrates that there were attempts to find out the facts, attempts were made to solve things peacefully, and the commanders issued orders to arrest anyone committing criminal acts. As for terror against civilians, I'll be very brief. It is our position that this requires special intent, and the Trial Chamber must establish special intent for every act and every defendant separately. Special intent cannot be established for the entirety of the judgement, nor can it be implied. Special intent may be established based on indicia as stated in the appeals judgement, Galic, paragraph 104, but it must be the only possible conclusion on the evidence. What misses in our judgement is any explicit finding, let alone reasoning, about the existence of special intent. I believe I still have up with more minute and if I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- we will reconvene in half an hour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, and good afternoon. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Todd Schneider for the Prosecution. Your Honours, General Petkovic's conviction rests on a solid foundation, contrary to what the Defence have argued. As chief and deputy chief of the HVO Main Staff, Petkovic deliberately and significantly contributed to the ethnic cleansing campaign in so many different ways: Planning and directing attacks and crimes to drive out Muslims, organising the expulsion of Muslims from Jablanica, ordering illegal forced labour, covering up his subordinates' crimes. And this is just a partial list of what he did to further the JCE. Why would he have done all this if there was no common criminal plan, as the Defence have argued today. As the Trial Chamber concluded, Petkovic was "one of the most important members of the JCE." Trial judgement, volume 4, paragraph 818. The Defence today have failed to undermine the reasonableness of this conclusion. And I will begin the Prosecution's response today by focussing on the Defence's challenges in Grounds 3 and 4 of their brief regarding Petkovic's JCE contribution and intent. The Chamber's conclusion that Petkovic was a JCE member was based on his wide-ranging and persistent pattern of criminal conduct throughout the entirety of the ethnic cleansing campaign; a pattern you've heard nothing about today from the Defence. Petkovic made so many contributions to the JCE that I'm going to focus on three main categories: Planning and directing attacks and crimes to drive out the Muslim population, being personally involved in expelling Muslims and other crimes, and covering up his subordinates' crimes or else turning a blind eye to their crimes. But before I discuss these contributions, let me first respond to some of the arguments from their brief on his powers as chief and deputy chief of the HVO Main Staff. Starting with Petkovic's authority over his HVO armed forces. What the Defence have argued in their briefs is that basically General Petkovic, the chief and deputy chief of the HVO Main Staff at the top of the HVO military chain of command, had no control over his own troops. This is simply implausible given the evidence in the record. As the Trial Chamber reasonably found, Petkovic had command and effective control over his troops. Volume 4, paragraph 679. This finding was amply supported most notably by his many orders to his troops. You see a list in front of you. This is a list of Petkovic orders cited in volume 4, paragraphs 661 through 678, in support of the Chamber's finding that he had command and effective control. More than 80 orders collected here. Covering deployment and combat readiness, offensive operations, inspections, investigations and discipline. The judgement is replete with examples of these orders being complied with. Volume 4, paragraphs 661 through 800. So in response to Defence argument that Petkovic's authority was limited, I would refer you to this list. When they suggest Mate Boban, the president and Supreme Commander, held all the real power over the armed forces, again I refer you to this list. Apart from this list, don't forget Petkovic's role in negotiations at the international level and with the ABiH, his role in implementing cease-fires, and his participation in strategic meetings with Croatian President Franjo Tudjman, VRS General Ratko Mladic, and others, all of which further supported the Chamber's findings on his authority and effective control.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My attention is being drawn that you are going too fast. Could you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Apologies to the interpreters especially. And just to conclude the citation, volume 4, paragraphs 18, 676 through 684. The Defence have raised a few more specific challenges to his authority. Let me address two of them now. First, they've argued that he lost command and control when he became deputy commander in July 1993. Again, this is the same list from before, with orders highlighted from when he was deputy commander or deputy chief. And just to highlight a few such orders, these include to shell the town of Mostar, to use prisoners for dangerous forced labour, to investigate and discipline; all showing Petkovic's command and control continued as deputy chief, as the Chamber reasonably found, volume 1, paragraphs 748 and 755. Now the Defence today have claimed that Petkovic had no authority over HVO detention centres; the Chamber's findings show otherwise. Of course, there are his illegal orders regarding dangerous forced labour, which I'll return to later. There's also his other orders, to release detainees, to regulate the treatment of prisoners. Volume 4, paragraphs 670, 788 through 800. To be clear, these so-called releases were often a pretext to expel Muslims and the orders on prisoners were insufficient to address the widespread detention crimes. They nevertheless demonstrate his power over detention centres. To sum up, there is no substance to Defence argument that Petkovic lacked authority over his own troops. So let's turn to how he used that authority. My next subject. Petkovic planned and directed attacks and crimes to drive out the Muslim population, one of his many contributions showing the Chamber reasonably found him to be a JCE member. The Chamber found that Petkovic engaged his forces in five municipalities, where they committed violent crimes against Muslims, in furtherance of the JCE; like in Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, and Jablanica, where his troops shelled the towns, set fire to Muslim homes, and forced Muslims out, all according to a preconceived plan; like in Mostar where he planned and ordered illegal shelling and his units violently evicted Muslims from their homes; like in Vares, where he sent in troops under Ivica Rajic, who then massacred dozens of Muslim civilians in Stupni Do and committed other crimes. Volume 4, paragraphs 693 through 767. Now, Defence today have challenged whether each of these five municipalities I've just mentioned form part of the common criminal purpose. We've responded in detail in our response brief to their factual challenges that you heard today on this point, but the Defence today have not mentioned -- they're ignored Petkovic's role in each -- in the attacks and crimes in each of these municipalities. And how his role undermines their arguments today that he favoured negotiations and peace. But let me address two of their challenges that they've raised in their appeal. First they have argued Petkovic took no part in the planning and directing of the attacks themselves. They would have you believe that the chief and deputy chief of the HVO Main Staff had no involvement in military operations spanning five municipalities. The Chamber reasonably found otherwise. In Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, and Jablanica, where in each municipality he personally deployed units. He received reports as the attacks unfolded. He ordered combat to cease. In Mostar, where he planned the shelling and the Main Staff took over the command of defending the town. In Vares, where he deployed the units. Volume 4, paragraphs 691 through 764. Given all this, the Chamber reasonably found Petkovic planned and directed these attacks. Another Defence argument is the claim that he didn't intend the crimes during and after these attacks. Now, the Defence haven't argued that Petkovic was unaware of crimes during and after these attacks, and in fact, as the Chamber reasonably found, Petkovic was repeatedly informed of his subordinates' crimes, such as destruction of property in Gornji Vakuf and Jablanica, violent evictions in Mostar. To list just some of these examples. Volume 4, paragraphs 710, 718, and 732. Given the clear evidence that Petkovic knew of his subordinates' crimes during and after the attacks, the Defence instead have made the following argument. They say there was no connection - no link - between these attacks and the violent crimes against Muslims in each municipality, as if they all spontaneously occurred at the same time. The Chamber reasonably found otherwise, because the same thing happened again and again when Petkovic sent in his troops, destruction of Muslim homes, illegal detentions of Muslim civilians, and other crimes, culminating in the expulsions of Muslims. The connection is clear between the attacks and the crimes, demonstrating it was reasonable for the Chamber to find Petkovic intended the crimes during and after these attacks, and that these attacks and crimes formed part of the common criminal plan. Volume 4, paragraphs 44 through 66 and 815. Now Petkovic's involvement in these attacks which started in January 1993 also rebuts the Defence argument today that prior to June 1993, Petkovic was merely interested in a joint command with the ABiH. His involvement rebuts their argument that he was merely seeking to have his HVO be allies with the ABiH. So let me turn to my next subject. Petkovic was personally involved in expelling Muslims and other crimes, another of the many contributions that show the Chamber reasonably found him to be a JCE member. Examples of his personal involvement include: Organising the forced removal of Muslims from Jablanica, ordering illegal arrests and detentions, planning the illegal shelling of East Mostar, and ordering and authorising the use of Muslim persons for illegal forced labour. See, for example, volume 4, paragraphs 723, 737, 750, and 793. None of which the Defence have raised or challenged today. But they have -- well, except for the first one, apologies. They have briefly noted the forced removal in Jablanica. Petkovic was personally involved in the expulsion of 450 Muslim women and children and elderly from Sovici and Doljani. The Defence concede Petkovic was involved in moving these civilians, but they have argued he did so on humanitarian grounds, because they wanted to leave. The Chamber reasonably rejected this explanation. After all, the victims had no choice in the matter. In large part, thanks to Petkovic himself. Because by the time they were moved, Petkovic's troops had already set fire to their villages, had already illegally detained them. Petkovic then went to Sovici and Doljani on 4 May, together with Pusic and others. He saw the burned-out houses. He saw deplorable conditions of confinement at Sovici school. So when Petkovic, through his orders, arranged for these civilians to be deported on buses from the school and other places where they were being detained, he was under no illusion that they were leaving of their own free will.
