Recall the end result, as one witness put it: Not a single Muslim was left in the Sovici and Doljani valley. Volume 2, paragraph 614; volume 4, paragraphs 717 through 724, and 1100 through 1104. Jablanica is compelling evidence showing the Trial Chamber reasonably found Petkovic intended to expel the Muslim population. So now let me turn to another example of his Petkovic's involvement that Defence have challenged at length today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: May I ask a question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel, for your argument. I am hearing what you say about acts of deportation and so on, but I would be grateful if you would refer in your argument now to the point made or which appeared to be made by the counsel for Mr. Petkovic earlier on, arguing in the context of joint criminal enterprise of ethnic cleansing, that basically the demographic composition of various contested localities has not changed. And from that she drew the conclusion, or appeared to draw the conclusion, that there was no ethnic cleansing. Could you help us in the Bench in how you understand this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours, if you give me just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Meron. I was planning to put that question myself later on, actually, because it is very pertinent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: In terms of the argument by the Defence this morning that you have referenced about the demographic composition not having changed, and that there was no ethnic cleansing, Your Honours, first, the ethnic map in a municipality doesn't need to change for a Trial Chamber to conclude that crimes within that municipality form part of the common criminal purpose. As the Djordjevic Appeals Chamber found at paragraph 154, the existence of a common criminal purpose doesn't depend upon proof that the purpose was achieved. So in this case the Chamber didn't need to ask it of it how many Muslims forcibly displaced in a municipality to conclude that crimes within the municipality were within the common criminal purpose. Instead, it was appropriate for the Chamber to rely on the similarity between HVO crimes across different municipalities to conclude crimes within all these municipalities were part of the common criminal purpose. And furthermore, in the end, the ethnic map of Herceg-Bosna did change, as tens of thousands of Muslims were forcibly displaced from Herceg-Bosna by HVO forces. And we've collected those findings in the Prosecution response brief to Petkovic at paragraph 43. So let me now turn to my next -- sorry. Apologies, Your Honour. Another example that the Defence have challenged today of his personal involvement is 30 June 1993 order that resulted in the illegal arrests and detentions of thousands of Muslim men, who were then terribly mistreated in HVO detention centres. I'm going to respond to most of the Defence arguments they've raised, and my colleague will then focus specifically on legal questions regarding the Muslim members of the HVO. The Defence claim this order was proper. They focussed a great deal today on the ABiH attack on 30 June 1993 and how this order was issued that same day. They focus on how he instructed that Muslim women and children be left in their homes. They don't talk about what happened before or after this order. They avoid how by the time of this order Petkovic had already planned and directed operations in two other municipalities: Gornji Vakuf and Jablanica, where his troops illegally arrested Muslims. They don't discuss how the thousands of Muslim men rounded up on this order were abused and mistreated once they entered the HVO detention centres. They avoid how Muslim women and children were rounded up and expelled during HVO operations taking place in the same municipalities at the same time. They don't talk about this bigger picture because if this really was a proper order from Petkovic, if this was just a temporary, makeshift response to the ABiH attack, we would expect to see the thousands of Muslim men rounded up being properly treated in HVO detention centres. Of course, that didn't happen. The two groups targeted by this order, the Muslim able-bodied men, the Muslim HVO members were arrested and detained along with all the other Muslim prisoners. They were beaten, kept in terrible conditions, and forced to work on the front lines. Finally, they were expelled from Herceg-Bosna. And see the judgement findings collected in our response brief at paragraph 152. Demonstrating Petkovic's order - targeted both of these groups because they were Muslims - as part of the ethnic cleansing campaign. So let me turn to Defence's arguments. First, the Muslim able-bodied men sometimes referred to as military-aged men. The Defence claim that the Muslim able-bodied men were members of the ABiH and they posed a legitimate security threat, so their arrests and detentions were proper. The Muslim able-bodied men were not members of an armed force. They were civilians. The general call to mobilisation in Bosnia, which the Defence rely on, was insufficient on its own to make the Muslim able-bodied men members of the ABiH. At most, this call to mobilise made them part of the reserves, conscripts as the Defence has said today. But, to be part of the ABiH, to lose their civilian status, a further step was required. The Muslim able-bodied men also had to be incorporated into the armed forces. Volume 3, paragraphs 618 through 620. What the Defence have relied on is simply not enough to make them members of an armed force. Given the Muslim able-bodied men were civilians, their detentions had to comply with international humanitarian law as to civilians. Which means, that for the security risk posed by the Muslim able-bodied men, Petkovic simply could not lump them together. Each Muslim male arrested had to be given the chance to challenge his detention on an individual basis. As the Appeals Chamber has held, there must be an assessment that each civilian in detention poses a particularly security risk. That's the Stanisic and Zupljanin appeals judgement, footnote 2953. The Muslim men were not assessed. They were abused, confirming that their arrests and detentions form part of the common criminal plan. Let me turn to some other Defence challenges that have been made to this order, that even if it wasn't implemented legally, at least Petkovic thought it would be. No, he didn't. I've already discussed how Petkovic planned operations where his troops illegally arrested Muslims. By the time of his mass arrest order, he had also been repeatedly informed that HVO forces were illegally detaining and abusing Muslim prisoners. Petkovic had also seen this first-hand just one month before the order at Sovici school. See the findings collected in our response brief at paragraph 81. He knew the same crimes would take place again once he issued this order. The Defence have made another argument today about Petkovic's awareness, that he issued this order on Boban's instructions. This is an irrelevant consideration. There is no following superior orders defence at this Tribunal as we've laid out in our response brief in paragraphs 92 through 95. Finally, the Defence try to absolve Petkovic of the widespread detention crimes resulting after his order by claiming that he had no responsibility for the thousands of Muslim men once they entered HVO detention centres. I've dealt with this earlier when I explained Petkovic did have authority over HVO detention centres. So he could have addressed the abuses against these prisoners. Instead, he chose not to. So let me turn to another example of Petkovic's personal involvement, his planning and ordering the illegal shelling of East Mostar. The Defence again talked about Mostar today but did not discuss Petkovic's role. Now, in their brief, the Defence have not challenged that "crimes were committed by shelling" at their reply brief paragraph 61, but they have argued Petkovic did not plan or order any of them. This is again the he-lacked-authority argument. The Chamber reasonably rejected this claim. Petkovic was in charge of HVO forces, including the artillery, throughout the illegal shelling of East Mostar. As I discussed before, Petkovic had command over all HVO forces. As I mentioned earlier, he had command over the HVO forces in Mostar. Indeed, the Main Staff took over the command of defending the town. Petkovic specifically had authority over HVO artillery. For example, the Siroki Brijeg artillery regiment was under the Main Staff's direct command from August to December 1993. This regiment directed fire at targets in Mostar, including the Old Bridge in September 1993. Volume 2, paragraph 1350. Petkovic also exercised his authority over HVO artillery. For example, he issued orders regarding HVO artillery in March and November 1993. Volume 4, paragraphs 745 and 746. The Defence have challenged in their briefs his November order, so let's just remind ourselves of the facts. On 8 November 1993, Petkovic ordered the HVO to shell the town of Mostar selectively at various intervals. His forces complied. An HVO tank deliberately targeted the Old Town, including by firing on the Old Bridge until it was destroyed on the 8th. The tank then continued to fire on the bridge on the 9th until it collapsed. Volume 4, paragraph 746 and 756; volume 2, 1306 through 1366. The Defence have said Petkovic never issued this order. The order on its face proves otherwise. This is the order itself, Exhibit P6534, cited at volume 4, paragraph 746. Look at the signature block: Milivoj Petkovic. There's no question. The Defence try to escape his own name on the page by saying, Look, there's no signature. But that's only because this version of the order was sent by packet communication through electronic channels. Documents sent this way never had a signature. Volume 1, footnote 1712. The Defence also claimed that Petkovic wasn't at Citluk from where the order was issued. But as the Chamber reasonably found, Petkovic issued this order remotely. At least one other order from Petkovic was issued remotely as well. See the findings at volume 2, paragraphs 607 and 1301. This order came from Petkovic. So let me turn to one more example of Petkovic's personal involvement that the Defence have ignored today. His illegal forced labour orders and authorisations. At least three such orders in July and August 1993. At least five such authorisations in October. The Defence say that what he did wasn't clearly illegal and that his orders weren't actually orders. Let me address each of these arguments. First they claim the dangerous forced labour in this case wasn't clearly illegal, that there was some ambiguity in the law, and that Petkovic acted in good faith when he ordered and authorised such labour. No. What he did was clearly illegal. Because he forced prisoners to work on the front lines, which is inherently dangerous and prohibited under international law. See volume 1, paragraphs 155 through 164, citing the relevant Articles of the Geneva Conventions. Petkovic knew this at the time. This is Exhibit P2950, cited in our response brief at paragraph 249. It's a June 1993 ICRC letter to Petkovic and others about the HVO sending prisoners to work in dangerous locations. "Such a practice is a serious break," they meant breach, "of the Geneva Conventions. It is" -- apologies, Your Honours, just waiting for the technical difficulty to be resolved. So let me start again. As the letter said: "Such a practice is a serious break of the Geneva Conventions. It is unacceptable and has to be stopped at once." Petkovic got this letter just three weeks before his 15 July order for prisoners to work on the front lines. So there is no ambiguity here about the illegality of this practice or Petkovic's awareness. So let me turn to another Defence argument. They say Petkovic's orders were not actually orders to have prisoners work on the front lines. Simply not true. Let's look at one of them. This is Petkovic's 8 August 1993 order discussed at volume 4, paragraph 800. Item 1 says: "Fortify the achieved lines immediately. Prisoners and detained Muslims may be used for fortifying lines." Recall that Coric executed this order. 100 Muslim detainees were sent out for labour on the front lines in line with Petkovic's order. Volume 4, paragraphs 800 through 801. Petkovic's July orders were similarly clear. In each one, he demanded that prisoners be used to fortify the defence lines. Volume 4, paragraph 790. Given such evidence, it was more than reasonable for the Trial Chamber to find Petkovic illegally ordered and authorised prisoners to work on the front lines. Volume 4, paragraphs 790 through 802. By doing so, he directly contributed to the "widespread, nearly systematic use" of detainees on the front lines for forced labour or as human shields, resulting in their murder or abuse. Volume 4, paragraph 66. In fact, the Chamber found that at least 33 prisoners were murdered during forced labour. Volume 3, paragraphs 676 and 683. There can be little surprise the illegal forced labour was so ubiquitous given it came straight from the top, from Petkovic himself. So let me turn to a new subject. Petkovic covered up his subordinates' crimes or else turned a blind eye to their crimes. Another of his many contributions that show the Chamber reasonably found Petkovic to be a JCE member. Petkovic ensured impunity for his subordinates' crimes in several different ways. Like the Stupni Do massacre in October 1993, where Petkovic ordered a sham investigation and helped Ivica Rajic stay in the HVO under a fake name. Like in Jablanica, where he ordered his troops to block passage of international observers and convoys so they could not visit the destroyed villages. Like with Tuta's Convicts Battalion and the Bruno Busic Regiment, whom he continued to use despite knowing of their crimes against Muslims. Volume 4, paragraphs 721, 777, and 804. Again, the Defence have ignored each of these today. First the Stupni Do cover-up. The Defence talked about the municipality of Stupni Do and the crimes there but not his role in covering them up. Recall the relevant facts. Petkovic's subordinates, led by Ivica Rajic, murdered 28 Muslim residents and destroyed all the houses in the village, following which Petkovic ordered an investigation into the massacre, to placate the international community. But the very same day, he sent a message to Rajic and called him to explain the investigation was just a formality, just a sham. Volume 3, paragraphs 480 through 484. Now, the Defence have argued Petkovic did not order a fake investigation. They've tried to poke holes in Witness EA's testimony about this. The Trial Chamber reasonably credited Witness EA because his testimony on this was so strongly corroborated by the other evidence. I've collected some of this evidence on a timeline which shows what happened between the massacre on 23 October 1993 and December 1993. First, Petkovic authored a message to Rajic about the sham investigation. Here you can see the handwritten note itself. The order for an investigation is merely as a formality. Returning to the timeline. Next, we see the Travnik deputy military prosecutor tried to investigate, but the local HVO brigades essentially provided no co-operation. Third, Rajic sent two reports to Petkovic, neither of which set out what actually happened during the massacre. And finally, Rajic assumed a fake name and continued to serve in the HVO despite Petkovic and others knowing of his involvement in the killings and other crimes. This evidence is cited at volume 3, paragraphs 480 through 495. Petkovic even admitted to knowing about Rajic's fake name. Given all this evidence, the Chamber reasonably relied on Witness EA's testimony when it found Petkovic ordered a fake investigation. So let me turn to another example of Petkovic covering up crimes in Jablanica. Recall that Petkovic planned and directed the attack and crimes there. He subsequently ordered his troops to block passage of international observers and convoys to conceal the crimes the HVO had committed in Sovici and Doljani. Volume 4, paragraph 721. The Defence do not deny that HVO blocked access for internationals. They have acknowledged there was a Main Staff order on 24 April to block an international convoy passing through Jablanica. Instead, they've tried to pass the buck, to shift the blame, by claiming the Main Staff order did not come from Petkovic himself because he was out of the country. The Chamber reasonably found this order did come from Petkovic based on his having planned and directed the attack in Jablanica, based on his knowledge of the crimes during and after this attack, based on Petkovic serving as the chief of the Main Staff at the time of the order. Volume 4, paragraph 721. I would just add the Chamber's findings elsewhere that Petkovic could issue orders from out of the country, like from Geneva in January 1993. Volume 2, paragraph 393. Given all this, the Chamber reasonably found that Petkovic ordered the cover-up in Jablanica. Let's turn to another example of the cover-ups or to his specifically turning a blind eye to subordinates' crimes. The Defence have said he didn't do this. They've gone through in great detail in their briefs a long list of orders that they claim were designed to prevent crimes, to ensure compliance with the laws of wars, to protect civilians. The truth is Petkovic protected his own with the cover-ups. As for the orders the Defence has cited, there were no teeth to them. They were just words on paper as his subsequent actions showed. Specifically his repeated deployment and use of HVO units that he knew had committed crimes against Muslims. Like the Bruno Busic Regiment, like the Convicts Battalion of Mladen Naletilic, also known as Tuta. And this is just a partial list of such units. Let me address here the Defence's arguments on these two units whom Petkovic used in locations such as Gornji Vakuf, Jablanica, and Mostar. Starting with the Bruno Busic Regiment. The Defence acknowledge that he could deploy and use this unit. Appeal brief, paragraphs 231, 239, obviously the Defence appeal brief. Their argument today is that Petkovic didn't know about the regiment's crimes. This ignores the evidence reasonably relied on by the Chamber. He personally deployed them in two attacks, Gornji Vakuf and Jablanica. He knew of the widespread crimes his forces committed against Muslims during and after these attacks. He specifically ordered the Bruno Busic Regiment to use Heliodrom detainees for illegal forced labour. Volume 4, paragraphs 809 through 811. Let me just briefly detour to Your Honours' question 4(c)(i) and the Defence argument on that point today. The Defence -- which relates to the Siljeg 28/29 January report, Exhibit P1351. The Defence have argued today that in response that Petkovic issued an order, P1344, to deal with the crimes in Jablanica -- sorry, in Gornji Vakuf. Trial Chamber reasonably rejected this interpretation of Petkovic's order, Exhibit P1344. They found that his continued use of this specific regiment, the Bruno Busic Regiment, shows that this order the Defence have cited today was not genuinely intended to punish and end the crimes against Muslims. And that's volume 4, paragraph 709. So let me turn next to -- sorry. Just to close out on the Bruno Busic Regiment. Based on the evidence I've just discussed -- the finding I just discussed, the Chamber found Petkovic was well aware of the regiment's criminality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Schneider, I see you looking at the clock repeatedly. You have ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honours. Next Tuta's Convicts Battalion and its ATGs, anti-terrorist groups. Here the Defence's arguments were reversed. They acknowledge that he knew of this unit's crimes. Appeal brief paragraph 257. But their argument has been he had no authority over them. He did not deploy and use them. Again, this ignores the evidence underlying the Chamber's findings. First, that Tuta's Convicts Battalion and its ATGs were explicitly within the HVO chain of command. Second, Petkovic and the Main Staff regularly deployed them. Volume 1, paragraphs 815 through 829. I want to focus here on one example. Petkovic's order, Exhibit P3128, from 2 July 1993, cited at volume 1, paragraph 828, where Petkovic ordered that "the Mostar ATG (from the Tuta ATG)" be used as part of the defence of the town of Mostar. Let me repeat: "The Mostar ATG (from the Tuta ATG)," and it's from page 2 of that exhibit. The Defence have challenged this order. They've noted Stojic co-signed this order as if this somehow undermined Petkovic's authority over the ATGs. They ignore other orders from Petkovic and the Main Staff regarding the Convicts Battalion and its ATGs that contain no co-signature from Stojic. And these are noted in our response brief at paragraph 125. In any event, the Defence argument misses the bigger picture. The bigger picture here is Petkovic's willingness to continue using Tuta's troops in Mostar despite his knowledge of their crimes. This order, Exhibit P3128, is from 2 July 1993. Just three weeks after Petkovic was informed that members of an ATG raped, abused, and evicted Muslims in Mostar. Just three months after Petkovic was informed that Tuta and his Convicts Battalion burned down Muslim homes in Jablanica and committed other crimes. Volume 4, paragraph 718 through 719, and 732. The bigger picture here is also what happened after this order. Members of Tuta's Convicts Battalion and its ATGs continued to commit crimes against Muslims in Mostar during the rest of 1993 and into 1994, violent expulsions, deaths, rapes, and sexual assaults, beatings of detainees and murders of detainees by forcing them to serve as human shields. Volume 2, paragraphs 977 through 987, 1609 through 1633. A telling example of how Petkovic turning a blind eye to his subordinates' crimes encouraged the commission of more crimes against Muslims, as the Chamber reasonably found. Volume 4, paragraph 816. And this is a good place to wrap up my discussion about Petkovic's contributions and intent because Petkovic's cover-ups, his turning a blind eye to his troops' crimes also make the broader point. There is no reason to punish your subordinates when they do exactly what you intend them to do. There's every reason to cover up their crimes when you're a member of the JCE. The Chamber's findings on Petkovic's JCE contributions and intent were eminently reasonable. The Defence's factual challenges in Grounds 3 and 4 should be dismissed. And, Your Honour, I believe that would bring us to the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I would be grateful if you would enlighten me on an aspect relevant to your argument and relevant to the argument made by the counsel of the Defence. We do know that under Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention either individual or group deportations are unlawful, and there is jurisprudence of the Tribunal to suggest that deportations can also be caused by other criminal behaviour. My question to you is: At what point of time do deportations transform into ethnic cleansing? How much of a population of an ethnic group you would have to expel in various ways, deport, in order to define the situation as ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Your Honour, to give a proper answer, I would request a chance to address it once we return from the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's no problem. No problem. Okay. No problem, Mr. Schneider, you'll deal with that after the break. Thank you, we'll reconvene at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, you have another hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon. I'd like to start about by coming back to Your Honour Judge Meron's question related to ethnic cleansing. The question asked at what point of time do deportations transform into ethnic cleansing? How much of a population of an ethnic group would you have to expel in order to define the situation as ethnic cleansing? As a preliminary matter, ethnic cleansing is not a crime provided for under the Statute or charged in this case. Judge Shahabuddeen in his partly dissenting opinion to the Stakic appeal judgement made this explicit: "Ethnic cleansing refers to a policy, this is not a crime in its own right under customary international law." And that's at paragraph 50. As the Appeals Chamber found in Stakic at paragraph 49: "Ethnic cleansing can involve the forcible displacement of civilians either across a border or across a front line." The crimes at the heart of an ethnic cleansing policy are therefore deportation and forcible transfer charged in this case under Counts 6 through 9. The term "ethnic cleansing" is in the indictment at paragraph 15 and the term is used by the Chamber at volume 4, paragraph 41, as part of the factual description of the common purpose. This factual characterisation is amply supported by the findings in this case that show the forced displacement of Muslims occurred on a massive scale. These same findings which I'm about to go through rebut the Defence's arguments today on demographics. So what were these findings? Many hundreds of Muslims were deported from West Mostar to East Mostar through waves of violent eviction operations between mid-May 1993 and February 1994. Volume 3, paragraph 782 through 783, and 853 through 856. As a result of HVO eviction operations in West Mostar, Stolac and Capljina, the population of East Mostar swelled from 20.000 in May 1993 to 55.000 in August 1993. Volume 2, paragraphs 1199 through 1200; volume 3, paragraph 853. In other words, 35.000 Muslims were expelled into East Mostar over the course of just four months. Several hundred Heliodrom prisoners were deported between July and November 1993, and several hundred more deported between the 15th and the 17th of December, 1993. And you can find that at volume 3, paragraphs 789 through 792. Hundreds were expelled from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Apologies again to the interpreters. Hundreds were expelled from Ljubuski to third countries in August 1993 through the system of deportation, conditioning release of the men on their agreement to leave BiH with their families. Volume 3, paragraph 793 through 795. The HVO deported hundreds of Gabela prisoners out of BiH in December 1993. Volume 3, paragraphs 807 through 809. At least 2500 women, children, and elderly were expelled from Prozor to ABiH territory on a single day, 28 August 1993. HVO soldiers rounded up the Muslim inhabitants of two villages, transported them toward the front line, and forced them to walk to ABiH-held territory while opening fire on the victims and wounding several people. Volume 3, paragraphs 840 through 842. Finally, between 6 or 7 July and 2 August 1993, the HVO arrested and detained women, children, and elderly Muslims from Stolac and expelled nearly 1250 of them to ABiH territory. The HVO then carried out another wave of arrests of women, children, and elderly from Stolac and after detaining them for several months, expelled them to ABiH territory in October, November 1993. Volume 3, paragraphs 881 through 883. So that would conclude our answer to that question as well as address the demographic arguments made earlier. So with that, I would just turn briefly to the other arguments made by the Defence this morning regarding the indictment. The Defence had notice of the JCE which the Chamber found had been established because it was well within the case pled in the indictment. I've already mentioned this but let me just read it out. The indictment expressly alleged "a joint criminal enterprise to politically and militarily subjugate, permanently remove, and ethnically cleanse Bosnian Muslims" and others. Again that was paragraph 15. So ethnic cleansing is directly contained in the indictment contrary to the Defence's argument today. The indictment further alleged that the appellants were responsible for all charged crimes pursuant to this JCE or, alternatively, pursuant to JCE 3. And that's at paragraphs 221 and 227 of the indictment. So there's no lack of notice to the Defence on these points. And with that, Your Honours, I would conclude my portion of the submissions and hand it to over to my colleague, Ms. Baig.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: I'd like to address Petkovic's argument concerning the fraction of the victims of the JCE crimes that are the detained Muslim victims who served in the HVO. The Trial Chamber made no error of fact or law in determining that the detained Muslims who had previously served in the HVO could be victims of grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions charged under Article 2 of the ICTY Statute. The key to the protections afforded by the Geneva Conventions to prisoners of war and civilians is the determination of whether the victims are in enemy hands. And this, of course, Your Honours, is determined by allegiance which in this case boils down to ethnicity. The Trial Chamber reasonably concluded that notwithstanding any prior or formal relationship with the HVO, these detained Muslims were at the time of the crimes in enemy hands. And here, Your Honours, I would like to point out this issue only concerns crimes that happened once the detainees were actually in custody. They had been disarmed and they were put into custody by the HVO. So this is the inhumane acts charged in Counts 13 and 16, concerning conditions of detention and mistreatment during detention, and Count 2, concerning killings in detention. So Petkovic's arguments this morning concerning the reasons for the arrest have no effect on these crimes. And once these victims were in enemy hands, then they were protected. And that's because the Geneva Conventions create a closed system. So by one Convention or another, once you're in enemy hands, you're a protected person. There are no gaps and there are no loopholes. So let me begin by explaining why the Trial Chamber was factually correct to conclude that the Muslim HVO detainees were in enemy hands and therefore protected persons. And I'll then explain why the Chamber's approach was correct on the law. As background, it's important to appreciate why there were Muslims in the HVO in the first place. You've heard a bit about this this morning. When the HVO was established in April 1992, its stated goals were to protect the territory, the Croatian people, as well as others in the community from aggression. Its ranks were not limited to Croats. Many Muslims joined or were otherwise mobilised into its armed forces. And in July 1992, Presidents Tudjman and Izetbegovic signed an agreement on friendship and co-operation which stated that the armed component of the HVO was an integral part of the united armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But by the beginning of 1993, Your Honours, when the JCE came into being and the crimes of this case began, this relationship of supposed friendship, based largely on the threat of the common Serb enemy, had deteriorated. And we see this very clearly when, after a series of clashes between the HVO and the ABiH, Prlic issues the January 1993 ultimatum, demanding the ABiH units to submit themselves to the command of the HVO Main Staff in the Croatian-claimed territories. And as the JCE came into being, the ethnic cleansing of the Muslims from the Croat-claimed territories began in earnest. As this ethnic separation objective became more clear, it is not surprising, Your Honours, that many of the Muslims, the Muslim members serving in the HVO, started to leave, and the Chamber found that they left in large numbers in May and June 1993. That's at volume 1 of the judgement, paragraph 776. As you heard this morning, on 30th of June, 1993, HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity who had deserted the HVO to then join the ABiH participated in an ABiH attack on the HVO's Northern Barracks in Mostar. And you can find the Chamber's finding at volume 2, paragraphs 878 to 886. Petkovic then ordered the mass arrest of all the Muslim men. He specified that all Muslims serving in the HVO shall be disarmed and placed in isolation, and he also ordered the arrest of all other able-bodied Muslim men in that area. And I should specify that's in the south-east OZ. This triggered a widespread and extensive campaign of arresting Muslim men with no distinction. ABiH Muslim soldiers, Muslims who had served or were serving in the HVO, and civilians, civilians as young as 14 up to the age of 84. And that's at volume 2, paragraphs 891 and 895. The arrests themselves, Your Honours, were organised and systematic and found to follow a recurring pattern. Many Muslim men were arrested from residential buildings, often at night, and then they were taken to temporary detention locations, such as the mechanical engineering faculty, before being transferred to larger detention centres, such as the Dretelj prison or the Heliodrom. And I refer you to volume 2, paragraph 893. And once in HVO custody, these Muslims were treated as one. No distinctions were drawn by the HVO on the basis of status. No distinctions were made between Muslim -- sorry, Muslim ABiH soldiers and those who had served in the HVO or even those who were in custody merely based on their supposed military age and nothing else. And no distinctions were made between Muslims who had served in the HVO and other Muslim detainees, no distinctions drawn in treatment between those who had deserted or those who were suspected of having participated in the attack on the Northern Barracks or anyone else. In contrast, detained Croat HVO soldiers, so, for example, those who had committed disciplinary infractions, were distinguished from the detained Muslims and held in separated quarters under better conditions. And this is noted in the judgement in volume 3, paragraph 199. And I'd also refer you to Witness E. The arrested Muslim men were held together in appalling conditions. They were beaten. They were sent to the front lines to do dangerous and life-threatening forced labour. Ultimately, many were expelled. And just like the other Muslim prisoners, the Muslims who had once served in the HVO were not permitted to challenge their detention regardless of status. And based on these factual findings, the Chamber reasonably concluded that the Muslim members of the HVO who were subsequently disarmed and then detained by the HVO were actually in enemy hands. And to make this determination, the Trial Chamber relied on the allegiance test set out in Tadic appeals judgement. That's Tadic appeals judgement of 1999 at paragraph 166. And in Tadic, the Appeals Chamber emphasised that this legal approach, hinging on substantial relations more than formal bonds, becomes all the more important in present-day international armed conflicts. So it's in accordance with this jurisprudence that the Trial Chamber took into account that from the time of the attack on the Northern Barracks on 30th June 1993, the HVO -- the HVO authorities themselves considered that the Muslim members of its ranks constituted a threat to security. Not on an individual basis, not because of anything that a single person had done, but rather, as an ethnic group. And, thus, Your Honour, the Chamber was reasonable to conclude that from at least 30th of June, 1993, the HVO Muslims were perceived by the HVO as loyal to the ABiH, the enemy. And that's at volume 3, paragraph 609 and 610. Once arrested and detained, they were factually in enemy hands. Volume 3, paragraph 611. And this makes sense. And the Chamber followed the logic -- the Chamber's logic follows the test that was approved in the Celebici Appeals Chamber. The Celebici appeals judgement at paragraph 98. In that case, as here, the victims were detained on the basis of their ethnicity and the victims were regarded by the perpetrators as now belonging to the opposing party and as posing a threat to the state. In both cases, they were in enemy hands. It's important to recall here that the crimes in this case in these detention centres occurred during an ongoing campaign of ethnic cleansing involving a widespread and systematic series of violent crimes against Muslims. And it's in that context that the HVO rounded up all the Muslims in its ranks, disarmed them, threw them into jail with all the other able-bodied Muslim men without distinction, subjected them to cruel and inhumane conditions of detention and mistreatment, and then used this detention as a means to expel the detainees from the claimed territory. And in these circumstances, Your Honours, it was reasonable for the Chamber to find that any bonds of allegiance that had previously existed were severed. At this point, all of the detained Muslims, including those who had initially served in the HVO, were factually in enemy hands. And legally, Your Honours, once a person is in enemy hands, then the remaining question is: Which Geneva Convention applies? The ICRC commentaries confirm that there are no gaps in the protections afforded by the Geneva Conventions. The 1958 commentary to Geneva Convention IV states: "Every person in enemy hands must have some status under international law ... there is no intermediate status; nobody in enemy hands can be outside the law." And that's at page 51. And the 1987 commentary to Additional Protocol I confirms this: "In armed conflict with an international character, a person of enemy nationality who is not entitled to prisoner-of-war status is, in principle, a civilian protected by the Fourth Convention, so that there are no gaps in protection." So once the Chamber determined that after being disarmed and imprisoned the Muslims who had served in the HVO were now in enemy hands, the Chamber had to figure out which of the conventions applied. It first addressed the more specific convention, the more specialised one, that is the Third Convention on prisoners of war and it found that its terms did not fit. The Chamber reasoned that the victims could not meet the requirement that they belonged to the adversary's armed forces, that is, the ABiH. So they were not prisoners of war under Geneva Convention III, and this analysis is set out at volume 3, paragraphs 603 and 604. This entirely consistent with the facts. These victims were never actually given any of the benefits of prisoner of war status and many of those benefits don't even work unless they're granted to a person who is actually a member of the adversary's armed forces, for example, benefits relating to ranks and notifications. So the Chamber moved on to consider Geneva Convention IV. And it found that once arrested, the Muslim men who had been members of the HVO were protected under the residual protections offered in Geneva Convention IV. And this is a legally sound conclusion. Although we generally think of Geneva Convention IV as the civilians convention, the express terms of its protection extend beyond the strict definition of a civilian. Although -- in Article 4, Geneva Convention IV defines protected persons as: "... those who, at any [sic] given moment and in any manner whatsoever, find themselves, in a case of conflict or occupation, in the hands of a party to the conflict or occupying power of which they are not nationals." So there's no mention of civilians in the definition of protected persons for the purpose of Geneva Convention IV. And the ICRC commentary explains that the definition in Article 4, paragraph 1 is "a very broad one." And that it includes members of the armed forces fit for service, wounded, sick, shipwrecked, who fall into enemy hands but who do not, for whatever reason, qualify for protection under the first three conventions. You can find that at page 50. So there's no inconsistency in the trial judgement. Geneva Convention IV's definition of who is in enemy hands is simply broader than that of Geneva Convention III. So it was correct and consistent for the Chamber to find, on the one hand, that these detainees were not prisoners of war because they were never actually formally part of the ABiH armed forces - that's at volume 3, paragraph 604 - but, on the other hand, that they were nevertheless protected under Geneva Convention IV where the enemy is defined more broadly by nationality or allegiance. And you can find that at paragraph 611 of volume 3. The Chamber's approach was fully in line with both the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and with international humanitarian law. My learned colleagues argued this morning that international humanitarian law does not apply to a party's own armed forces. But this argument is both irrelevant and inaccurate. It's irrelevant because at the time of the crimes, these soldiers were factually determined by the Trial Chamber to be in the hands of the enemy. So for the purposes of the Geneva Conventions, they were no longer a party's own soldiers. And this argument is also inaccurate because it's an oversimplification. There is no such bright-line rule. On the contrary, there are war crimes, such as the grave breaches in Geneva Conventions I and II, that are not limited to persons who are in enemy hands and that do expressly include crimes against a party's own soldiers. And I would refer you to Geneva Convention I, Article 12. Likewise, Your Honours, crimes based on Common Article 3's minimum protections would apply to members of the armed forces victimised by their own party. And I would refer you to the ICRC's 2016 commentary to Geneva Convention I which confirms that Common Article 3 serves as a minimum yard-stick reflecting elementary considerations of humanity which also applies to a party's own armed forces. And you can find that at paragraphs 547 to 549. Common Article 3 does not require the victim to be in the hands of the enemy. And for this reason, if Your Honours were to reverse either of the grave breaches of inhumane acts counts, that's Counts 13 and 16, then we would ask you to substitute Counts 14 and 17. These are the corresponding cruel treatment violations of the laws and customs of war based on Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions. The Trial Chamber has already made all the necessary findings for these counts but it did not enter convictions because they were found to be impermissibly cumulative of the Article 2 charges. I would also note here, Your Honours, that similar fundamental guarantees to Common Article 3 applying to a party's own forces are set out in Article 75 of Additional Protocol I, and for its application to the present situation, I would also refer you to Article 45(3). And, so Your Honours, the Trial Chamber's conclusion that the detained Muslims who had served in the HVO were protected persons was correct in both fact and law. Subject to any questions you might have, I will pass the floor now to my colleague Ms. Elmore, who would like to answer question 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELMORE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Elizabeth Elmore for the Prosecution. I will be addressing question number 8 of the appeal preparation order in which Your Honours asked whether, in convicting Petkovic of the crime of unlawful infliction of terror on civilians, the Trial Chamber made the necessary findings on his specific intent to spread terror and what the impact would be if the Appeals Chamber found that the Trial Chamber failed to provide a reasoned opinion in this regard. This relates to Ground 3 of Petkovic's appeal. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber made the necessary findings to establish that Petkovic possessed the specific intent to inflict terror on civilians. At volume 4, paragraph 820, the Chamber concluded that Petkovic was criminally responsible as a member of a joint criminal enterprise for the crime of terror. The judgement does not contain a separate finding on his specific intent but this conclusion has to be read into the Trial Chamber's ultimate conclusion that he was individually criminally responsible for the crime of terror. And the reason for this is because the Trial Chamber was aware of the requirements for the crime of terror, including specific intent, and of the requirements of JCE responsibility. And because the Trial Chamber then made extensive factual and legal findings throughout the judgement reflecting Petkovic's specific intent to inflict terror. First, in volume 1, the Chamber correctly set forth that the mens rea for terror requires the specific intent to spread terror as the primary purpose. That's volume 1, paragraph 197. Then, in volume 3, the Trial Chamber found that the HVO committed the crime of terror in East Mostar by committing acts of violence with the specific intent to inflict terror on civilians as their primary purpose. That's volume 3, paragraphs 1691 to 1692. And here I would just like to emphasise something in relation to Your Honours' earlier question on this point. It is not the Prosecution's position that the volume 3 finding on the HVO's specific intent to spread terror is sufficient reasoning to establish Petkovic's specific intent. Rather, it's simply one of several steps in the Trial Chamber's reasoning that led to its ultimate conclusion that Petkovic intended the crime of terror in East Mostar. And this conclusion and the reasoning for it is in volume 4. Here the Trial Chamber expressly found that the crime of terror formed part of the common criminal purpose, that's at paragraph 68, and that Petkovic intended this crime be committed. That's at paragraph 815. And in support of its conclusion that Petkovic intended this crime, it made specific findings about his direct contributions to and knowledge of the terror campaign. I'll go through these in more detail in a moment, but, briefly, the Trial Chamber found that Petkovic knew about the HVO crimes in East Mostar, that he was obviously aware that these crimes terrorised civilians, that he personally planned and ordered HVO crimes that terrorised civilians, and, that, therefore, he intended the HVO's crimes in East Mostar. That's volume 4, paragraph 750 to 756. Your Honours, these findings constitute a reasoned opinion for Petkovic's conviction for the crime of terror. They reflect the Trial Chamber's conclusion that he had the specific intent to spread terror. Read as a whole, the Trial Chamber correctly understood the legal issue to be determined and gave sufficient reasons for its conclusions. There is no failure to provide a reasoned opinion. However, if Your Honours do conclude that a discrete specific intent finding was required, Your Honours can correct any oversight by simply making express in the appeal judgement what is already evident in the trial judgement and Your Honours can do so based on the findings of the Trial Chamber alone. Because the only reading of these findings is that the Trial Chamber was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Petkovic specifically intended to inflict terror on civilians. And here I would refer you to the Naletilic appeal judgement, paragraph 122; the Lukic and Lukic appeal judgement, paragraphs 437 to 440, and 459 to 461; and the Stanisic and Zupljanin appeal judgement, paragraphs 356, 376, and 378. These are all cases in which an Appeals Chamber upheld the Trial Chamber's ultimate conclusion even though a necessary finding was not explicitly set out in the trial judgement. In each of these cases, the Appeals Chamber considered that the trial judgement read as a whole demonstrated that the Trial Chamber had determined the issue in question. And if Your Honours deem it necessary, it is certainly open to this Chamber to go to the record and review the underlying evidence to satisfy itself that the Trial Chamber's ultimate conclusion was correct. This would lead Your Honours to the same inescapable conclusion: Petkovic possessed the specific intent to inflict terror on the civilians of East Mostar. So let me first take a moment to go through some of the Chamber's relevant findings on what the HVO did to these civilians and why it concluded that their primary purpose was to terrorise them. Then I will address why Petkovic himself shared that intent. First of all, HVO snipers deliberately shot civilians and shot at them for nine straight months. And not just women, not just the elderly, they deliberately shot children. They shot a boy named Orhan Berisa in the back. He managed to crawl to safety out of the line of fire but he still died later that same day. And he was 8 years old. That's volume 2, paragraphs 1060, 1154, 1163; and volume 3, paragraph 1689. For nine straight months, HVO heavy artillery shelled East Mostar civilians on average 20 to 100 times per day. The HVO used planes to drop napalm bombs on civilians and fired tires filled with explosives at their homes. They struck at the very heart of the Muslim population's cultural and religious life by deliberately demolishing ten mosques and the Old Bridge. That's volume 2, paragraphs 1000, 1005 to 1006; and volume 3, paragraphs 1689 to 1690. Moreover, the HVO violently forced over 30.000 Muslims who had been evicted from other places into overcrowded East Mostar and then incrementally tightened the vise in which they had trapped them. In addition to the sniping and shelling campaign, they intentionally aggravated the brutal living conditions there, isolating them and impeding the delivery of desperately needed humanitarian aid. As the Trial Chamber reasonably found, living day in and day out under the constant threat of death or injury, in fact, terrified the population. That's volume 2, paragraphs 1015, 1199 to 1200; and volume 3, paragraphs 1689 to 1692. Your Honours, the evidence and the findings on the events in East Mostar support only one conclusion, the one that the Trial Chamber reached, that the primary purpose of the HVO's acts of violence there was to inflict terror on the civilian population. So let me turn to the Trial Chamber's findings on Petkovic. In concluding that Petkovic intended this terror, the Trial Chamber relied on his knowledge of these acts of violence intended to inflict terror, on his direct contributions to inflicting this terror, and on his awareness of the actual terror inflicted. So let me take Your Honours through these findings. First we should be clear who these HVO forces were who committed acts of violence with the primary purpose of terrorising civilians. So these HVO forces who shelled terrified families for nine straight months, who shot an 8-year-old boy in the back, these were Petkovic's troops, his subordinates. As Mr. Schneider already explained, Petkovic was the chief and then deputy commander of the HVO Main Staff during the relevant time-period. He exercised command and control authority and effective control over the HVO forces in East Mostar during the siege. That's volume 4, paragraph 814. And what did Petkovic do with his power over these forces? He planned and ordered the very HVO shelling attacks that the Chamber found were undertaken with the primary purpose of terrorising civilians, attacks that killed and injured civilians and destroyed mosques. In fact, he ordered the very offensive in which the HVO shelled the Old Bridge until it collapsed. Petkovic also personally impeded the delivery of humanitarian aid and the access of international organisations trying to help the trapped civilians. That's volume 4, paragraphs 745 to 756. Moreover, there's no doubt that he knew about not just the existence of the terror campaign but the sheer magnitude of it. International witnesses told Petkovic directly and repeatedly that his troops were targeting both the civilian population and the members of international organisations on the ground trying to help them. For example, the SpaBat leadership went to Petkovic again and again about his troops' attacks on both civilians and SpaBat personnel. As the Chamber thus found, Petkovic knew of the resulting deaths, injury and destruction, and was obviously aware of the terror inflicted on the civilian population. That's volume 4, paragraphs 748 to 750. And his response was to continue contributing to the common criminal purpose. And he actually encouraged the commission of subsequent crimes by continuing to deploy perpetrators to the field, rather than trying to stop or punish them. That's volume 4, paragraphs 815 to 816. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber looked at Petkovic's knowledge of the terrorisation of East Mostar civilians, at his direct contributions to the terrorisation of these civilians, and at his decision to keep on contributing to the common criminal purpose, and the Trial Chamber concluded that the only inference it could reasonably draw was that Petkovic intended the crime of terror be committed there. Volume 4, paragraph 815. Your Honours, these findings constitute a reasoned opinion and they clearly reflect the Trial Chamber's conclusion that Petkovic specifically intended the terrorisation of these civilians. However, if Your Honours do take the view that the Trial Chamber erred by not making a discrete specific intent finding, we would urge this Chamber not to leave Petkovic's criminal responsibility for this terror unadjudicated. Your Honours can safely rely on the Trial Chamber's underlying findings or go to the underlying evidence, if needed, but Petkovic should not be acquitted of this crime due to a lack of a specific intent finding by the Trial Chamber. Petkovic and his troops trapped over 55.000 civilians in East Mostar and then terrorised them for months on end. Those civilians deserve a final adjudication of his responsibility for it. If there are no questions, Your Honours, that will conclude my submissions and to conclude -- for all the reasons set out in our brief and argued today, Petkovic's appeal should be dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's all? That's all, okay. Defence for Mr. Petkovic. You have 30 minutes starting from now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, good day to everyone in the courtroom. Your Honours, we shall commence our answer with the topic how many residents of an area have to be expelled in order to find ethnic cleansing? Please look at an excerpt from the Prosecution's response, where he states that ethnic cleansing does not necessarily have to be committed in order to find that the criminal intent of ethnic cleansing has been accomplished. It's still not on the screen. That's what the Prosecution cites in paragraph 42 of their response, and my learned friend Mr. Schneider also said today that it is not necessary for ethnic cleansing to have been committed for something to be deemed committed with the criminal intent of ethnic cleansing. The Prosecution cited the appeals judgement from the Djordjevic case, paragraph 154. You will see from this passage that the Prosecution simply misquoted this judgement and claimed that something exists in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. This paragraph actually says that ethnic cleansing needs not have been committed on a permanent basis. It can be only temporarily achieved for the criminal intent of ethnic cleansing to hold. The Prosecution and the Defence team of General Petkovic have spent already a lot of time on this, and that's why in my introduction I put an excerpt from the Djordjevic judgement where it states that ethnic cleansing has to be accomplished for the criminal intent of ethnic cleansing to stand. The Prosecution conceived their response in such a way that with regard to one accused, they cover topics raised by other Defences. I'm now going to digress a little from today's response of the Prosecution and spend one minute on the maps shown to us by the Prosecution in this courtroom. They showed us a map of Herceg-Bosna and the map of Banovina from 1993, and that was supposed to be proof that there was an intention to recreate the Banovina in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, to these maps we added the map of the territorial organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina under the Vance-Owen Plan from January 1993 and a map of the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan from August 1993. With a margin of error plus/minus 10 per cent of the territories, these are identical maps. Because this concerns territories with the majority Croat population. Your Honours, if we asked Mr. Serge Brammertz this very minute to organisation territorially Bosnia-Herzegovina taking into account the ethnic makeup of the population, he would produce a very similar map. Now, I would like to say a few words on the topic of occupation covered by the Defence of General Praljak, speaking about the conflict in general, but I wish to make four points on the topic of occupation that I believe are very important. First of all, the topic of occupation is important not only with regard to the crimes from Count 19 of the indictment, as asserted by the Prosecution, it's also important to Counts 7 and 9 because these crimes are crimes of transfer and deportation that can concern only the civilian population, and then the issue is whether the state of occupation is actual and relevant. The Trial Chamber established beyond a reasonable doubt that there was a war from May 1993 until spring 1994. If we start from the premise that warfare excludes a state of occupation, then crimes from Counts 7, 9 and 19 could not have been committed in the territory of Mostar. Another point on occupation we believe is important is this. The Trial Chamber adopted the criteria from the Naletilic judgement which held that a state of occupation was established, and it was in judgement, volume 1, paragraph 88. However, in our view, the Chamber erroneously found that all these criteria do not have to be met cumulatively. Our position is, from interpreting the Naletilic judgement, paragraph 587, that these criteria must be met cumulatively. It is our view that had the Trial Chamber applied these criteria cumulatively, they would not have found a state of occupation in the relevant areas. The third important thesis for us today is this. We deem indubitable the stand of jurisprudence that a state of war exists and a state has overall control over forces in another state. We also find indubitable that occupation exists if an occupation force, that is to say, another state, has effective control over a territory that is considered to be occupied. Our Trial Chamber, in fact its majority, introduced through the back door via a state agent a change to this rule and determined the following: That Croatia had overall control over the HVO without bothering to determine the effective control of Croatia. It still found that Croatia was an occupation force in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We believe that a state of occupation determined in this way is simply incorrect and that it is an erroneous application of law that invalidates the judgement. And, finally, speaking of occupation willy-nilly, we bear in mind the authority of the occupation commander as the occupation governor and we perceive the tasks and authorisations of the commander differently than we would in a situation where there is no occupation. And that affected directly, in our view, the perception of the role and responsibility of General Petkovic as the commander of the HVO. Just a few words about Mostar and the claim made both in the judgement and by the OTP today that Petkovic ordered the shelling of Mostar and that he is, therefore, liable for the crime of terror against civilians. Your Honours, the whole story about Petkovic's participation in the shelling of Mostar is based on Exhibit P6534, which is an order that we've seen today on our screens, not signed but goes under the name of General Petkovic dated 8 November, and the Prosecution claims it's an order by Petkovic based on which the Old Bridge was destroyed. We wish to tell you, Your Honours, that the Prosecutor made this claim for the first time in their final brief. To tell you the truth, we were shocked because, at that moment, until that moment, neither we nor General Petkovic heard that he was ever directly linked to the destruction of the Old Bridge. That's why we, the Defence of General Petkovic, had never dealt with the subject at all. It was only in our closing arguments that we had to prove it's not a document issued by General Petkovic. From the evidence in the case, and we spoke of this in detail in our appeal brief, it is indubitable that General Petkovic was in Split on that day; 4D2026, 4D2026 [as interpreted], and the testimony of General Praljak, transcript 41270. There is absolutely no doubt that under the name of General Petkovic a number of other documents were issued, including one order, 4D834. General Praljak, in his testimony, said that this document that went out under Petkovic's name was not issued by Petkovic, nor was it signed by him. The testimony of General Praljak, T41270. Let us look at how our Trial Chamber evaluated this evidence. Judgement, volume 2, paragraph 1301. The Chamber stated as follows: "Petkovic could have issued that order from Split as well. The Chamber had no proof that Petkovic had not done so from Split and, therefore, concluded that he did." This is, Your Honours, believe it or not, a verbatim quotation from the judgement on such an important issue as whether Petkovic did or did not issue the order to destroy the Old Bridge. Now on the topic of Stupni Do. We do not argue that crimes were committed, certainly not, but we wish to point out the following circumstances. Also thanks to an order by General Petkovic, the representatives of the international community, including the UNPROFOR, entered Stupni Do two days later; P6078. These alleged crimes, because nothing was known exactly at that time, were notified to General Petkovic by General Ramsey; P6144. On the 2nd November 1993, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina took Vares. We have discussed this today. Thus, two days after the commission of the crimes in Stupni Do, overall control of the area where the crimes were committed was in the hands of the international community representatives and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Nobody from the HVO, including General Petkovic, was able to do anything to prevent the crimes from being investigated. This inquiry and the whole control was in the hands of the representatives of the international community and the ABH. What is in issue for my client is whether he did or did not participate in identifying the people responsible for the crimes and in punishing them. On this point, we wish to emphasise that it was the Prosecution that conducted the investigation of the crimes in Stupni Do. Documents 4D499; 4D500; the testimony of Witness EA; Witness Bandic; and Petkovic. I can refer you to footnote 398 of the Petkovic appeal brief. The top commander of the HVO, Mate Boban, was familiar with all the information available to the HVO at that time, as did the then-Defence minister Jukic. We detailed this in paragraph 290 to 294 of our appeal brief. What is true, Your Honour, is that the top commander of the HVO, Mate Boban, decided that Commander Ivica Rajic should remain in his position but change his name to Viktor Andric. And the reasons for this decision were this: They wanted to deceive the representatives of the international community into believing that the person responsible for the crimes had been removed from their position while retaining the commander, whom the top commander considered to be the only one able to ensure that the HVO not lose control over Kiseljak. This fact was known to my client, General Petkovic. He bears his part of the responsibility for this awareness, but the fact stands that that he, from his position of chief of Main Staff, was unable to take any steps against it at the time. May I make a correction? On page 90, line 2, it's not chief of Main Staff. It's deputy chief of Main Staff. Your Honours, I think that I still have nine minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have ten, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Ten, okay. Good. [Interpretation] Just a few words about the Bruno Busic units and the Convicts Battalion for which, in the judgement, the Trial Chamber established that they committed crimes and that by engaging those units in certain military actions Petkovic contributed to the implementation of the criminal purpose. And we discussed this in detail and we contested these arguments in detail in our appeal, paragraphs 331 to 351. And I hope that you will take that into account. A few words about the Bruno Busic unit. There is no document in the case file, no report indicating that the Bruno Busic unit committed any crimes in Gornji Vakuf in January of 1993. When I say "document," I mean a document that was issued in 1993, in January or subsequently in 1993, and which could have objectively been accessible to anyone at the Main Staff. I see my colleague Mr. Stringer is looking for facts, so I can say that this assertion by the Trial Chamber is based on a document of the ABiH drafted in late 1993 and on two testimonies of Prosecution witnesses. Thus, there is no document unless I made an oversight in my analysis and I don't think that I did. We can say that no document dating from the first half of 1993 exists indicating that the Bruno Busic unit committed any crimes in Jablanica in April 1993. The Trial Chamber itself established - and I don't want to be too detailed here - that a number of soldiers from that unit were present in the territory where mistreatments of imprisoned Muslim soldiers occurred, but there is not a single word indicating that members of the Bruno Busic Brigade committed any crime. Thus, any assertions about the engagement of this unit in some military operations with the objective of permitting or carrying out any criminal acts is unfounded. As for the convicts unit, which really was a very problematic one, we attempted to prove, in the course of five years in the courtroom, that this unit was a part of the HVO but that it was directly subordinated to the Supreme Commander, Mate Boban, and that Milivoj Petkovic did not have direct control over that unit. If you look at what the Prosecution said on this topic today, you will see that they referred to one single document only dated the 2nd of July, 1993. This is document P3128. But the Prosecution also noted that Petkovic was not the only signatory of the document. It is our position that that document does not provide any grounds for a rational and founded conclusion that the Convicts Battalion was directly under the command of the Main Staff and that the assertions of the Defence [as interpreted] are incorrect that the unit was directly subordinated to the Main Staff -- to the Supreme Commander. I correct the transcript. Line 21, it should be assertion by the Prosecution. Very well. I cannot be following the transcript at the same time. To move on. Our colleague Mr. Schneider also drew an equal sign between two things: The planning of military actions and the planning of crimes. The Trial Chamber also did that. So the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution said, You were planning a military operation and crimes occurred as part of that military operation. Therefore, you planned military crimes. We consider this to be just a logical error, and this manner of drawing conclusions cannot lead to any valid conclusion. We can look at General Petkovic's orders, all of the orders of General Petkovic, which are in Annex 4 of our final trial brief. Your Honours, we tried to provide to the Trial Chamber what kind of orders General Petkovic issued. So if you look at line one, these are commands on military activities. There are two up to 1993 and there are ones that were issued subsequently. If we analysed them in detail, you will see that there are no orders there relating to military actions or military operations. These are mostly types of orders, fortify lines, logistics, strengthen the lines and so on and so forth. An analysis like this about the content of the orders indicates that the HVO did not plan nor did it conduct assault offensive actions against the ABiH. And the structure of all the orders indicates that the HVO reacted to the actual situation in the field, that it tried to strengthen some lines of defence, and that it was simply attempting to save the situation that was in force at that particular moment. So we believe that this document contradicts the assertion about planning military actions in which crimes were committed and therefore the conclusion that thereby crimes were planned. Finally, I wanted to talk about Jablanica, Sovici and Doljani. The Prosecution stated a number of times during these past four days that in early May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have less than one minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That in early May in Sovici, Petkovic, Pusic, and others were present, and these others are General Sefer Halilovic, Arif Pasalic, and representatives of the international community. All of them together were touring the terrain and trying to ascertain the status there and to assist the population to the necessary degree. At Halilovic's request, the HVO provided assistance that Halilovic needed. Your Honours, thank you very much. Thank you.
